Reference: Gonzales, Ito and Reguant (2023)

Research Question

The paper studies how electricity market integration affects renewable energy through two distinct channels:

Market Integration→Gains from Trade+Investment Effects.(8.2.1.1)\text{Market Integration}\rightarrow\text{Gains from Trade}+\text{Investment Effects}. \tag{8.2.1.1}Market Integration→Gains from Trade+Investment Effects.(8.2.1.1)

The first channel holds generation capacity fixed and studies the reallocation of electricity production across regions. The second channel allows transmission expansion to change the profitability of renewable investment and therefore the long-run generation capacity. The key empirical point is that renewable investment may occur in anticipation of future market integration, so a standard before-and-after comparison may fail to capture the full effect.

Stylized Two-Region Model

There are two regions, r∈{A,B}r\in\{A,B\}r∈{A,B} with fixed demands DA,DBD_A,D_BDA​,DB​. Let nonsolar production in each region be qA,qBq_A,q_BqA​,qB​. Marginal generation costs are linear:

CA(qA)=βAqA;CB(qB)=βBqB(8.2.1.2)C_A(q_A)=\beta_A q_A;\qquad C_B(q_B)=\beta_B q_B \tag{8.2.1.2}CA​(qA​)=βA​qA​;CB​(qB​)=βB​qB​(8.2.1.2)

Assume βA≤βB\beta_A\leq\beta_BβA​≤βB​, so region AAA is the relatively low-cost region.

Autarky Equilibrium

Without transmission between the two regions, qA=DAq_A=D_AqA​=DA​, qB=DBq_B=D_BqB​=DB​. Therefore,

pA=βADA;pB=βBDB.(8.2.1.3)p_A=\beta_A D_A;\qquad p_B=\beta_B D_B. \tag{8.2.1.3}pA​=βA​DA​;pB​=βB​DB​.(8.2.1.3)

The model focuses on the case pA<pBp_A<p_BpA​<pB​. Region AAA therefore has lower electricity prices before integration.

Market Integration Without Investment Effects

Define aggregate demand as D=DA+DBD=D_A+D_BD=DA​+DB​. Under full market integration, electricity can flow freely between the two regions. Cost minimization implies equal marginal costs:

βAqA=βBqB=p∗,qA+qB=D(8.2.1.4)\beta_A q_A=\beta_B q_B=p^*,\qquad q_A+q_B=D \tag{8.2.1.4}βA​qA​=βB​qB​=p∗,qA​+qB​=D(8.2.1.4)

which gives

p∗=βAβBβA+βBD,qA=βBβA+βBD,qB=βAβA+βBD(8.2.1.5)p^*=\frac{\beta_A\beta_B}{\beta_A+\beta_B}D,\qquad q_A=\frac{\beta_B}{\beta_A+\beta_B}D,\qquad q_B=\frac{\beta_A}{\beta_A+\beta_B}D \tag{8.2.1.5}p∗=βA​+βB​βA​βB​​D,qA​=βA​+βB​βB​​D,qB​=βA​+βB​βA​​D(8.2.1.5)

Market integration therefore reallocates production toward the lower-cost region. This is the conventional gains-from-trade effect:

Transmission Expansion→Reallocation of Existing Generation→Lower Generation Cost.(8.2.1.6)\text{Transmission Expansion}\rightarrow\text{Reallocation of Existing Generation}\rightarrow\text{Lower Generation Cost}. \tag{8.2.1.6}Transmission Expansion→Reallocation of Existing Generation→Lower Generation Cost.(8.2.1.6)

Endogenous Solar Investment

Suppose solar generation can be built only in region AAA. Solar has approximately zero marginal operating cost but requires an upfront investment.

Let ccc denote the price level required to make solar investment profitable. Assume pA<c<p∗p_A<c<p^*pA​<c<p∗, then solar investment is not profitable under autarky but becomes profitable after market integration.

With competitive entry, solar capacity expands until profits are driven to zero. The long-run equilibrium price therefore satisfies p∗∗=cp^{**}=cp∗∗=c. At this price, nonsolar production is

qA=cβA,qB=cβB(8.2.1.7)q_A=\frac{c}{\beta_A}, \qquad q_B=\frac{c}{\beta_B} \tag{8.2.1.7}qA​=βA​c​,qB​=βB​c​(8.2.1.7)

Solar production supplies the residual demand:

qsolar=D−qA−qB.(8.2.1.8)q_{\mathrm{solar}}=D-q_A-q_B. \tag{8.2.1.8}qsolar​=D−qA​−qB​.(8.2.1.8)

Hence,

qsolar=D−βA+βBβAβBc.(8.2.1.9)\boxed{q_{\mathrm{solar}}=D-\frac{\beta_A+\beta_B}{\beta_A\beta_B}c}. \tag{8.2.1.9}qsolar​=D−βA​βB​βA​+βB​​c​.(8.2.1.9)

Market integration therefore changes not only the allocation of existing production but also the equilibrium generation capacity.

Investment Effect

The key mechanism is

Transmission Capacity↑→Ability to Export Solar Electricity↑(8.2.1.10)\text{Transmission Capacity}\uparrow\rightarrow\text{Ability to Export Solar Electricity}\uparrow \tag{8.2.1.10}Transmission Capacity↑→Ability to Export Solar Electricity↑(8.2.1.10)
→pA↑→Expected Solar Revenue↑→Solar Investment↑.(8.2.1.11)\rightarrow p_A\uparrow\rightarrow\text{Expected Solar Revenue}\uparrow \rightarrow\text{Solar Investment}\uparrow. \tag{8.2.1.11}→pA​↑→Expected Solar Revenue↑→Solar Investment↑.(8.2.1.11)

Hence the long-run gains from market integration contain an additional investment effect that is absent from a model with fixed generation capacity.

Anticipatory Investment

Transmission projects are announced and constructed several years before they become operational. Investors can therefore build solar plants before market integration actually occurs. Suppose the equilibrium quantity of solar induced by future integration is already installed, but the two regions are still separated. Region AAA then produces only the residual nonsolar demand:

qA=DA−qsolar.(8.2.1.12)q_A=D_A-q_{\mathrm{solar}}. \tag{8.2.1.12}qA​=DA​−qsolar​.(8.2.1.12)

Substituting the equilibrium solar quantity gives

qA=βA+βBβAβBc−DB(8.2.1.13)q_A=\frac{\beta_A+\beta_B}{\beta_A\beta_B}c-D_B \tag{8.2.1.13}qA​=βA​βB​βA​+βB​​c−DB​(8.2.1.13)

The resulting pre-integration price in region AAA is

p~A=βAqA(8.2.1.14)\widetilde p_A=\beta_A q_A \tag{8.2.1.14}p​A​=βA​qA​(8.2.1.14)

or

p~A=(1+βAβB)c−βADB(8.2.1.15)\boxed{\widetilde p_A=\left(1+\frac{\beta_A}{\beta_B}\right)c-\beta_A D_B} \tag{8.2.1.15}p​A​=(1+βB​βA​​)c−βA​DB​​(8.2.1.15)

Because solar capacity has already entered, we have p~A<pA\tilde{p}_A<p_Ap~​A​<pA​. Thus the “pre-treatment” equilibrium may already reflect the future transmission expansion.

Implication for Event Studies

Anticipatory investment implies

Pre-Period Outcome≠No-Policy Counterfactual.(8.2.1.16)\text{Pre-Period Outcome}\neq\text{No-Policy Counterfactual}. \tag{8.2.1.16}Pre-Period Outcome=No-Policy Counterfactual.(8.2.1.16)

This generates three main predictions. First, the observed reduction in generation costs around the transmission opening tends to understate the full long-run cost reduction:

Event-Study Cost Effect<Full Cost Effect(8.2.1.17)\text{Event-Study Cost Effect}<\text{Full Cost Effect} \tag{8.2.1.17}Event-Study Cost Effect<Full Cost Effect(8.2.1.17)

Second, the observed reduction in electricity prices tends to understate the full price effect because solar entry has already depressed pre-integration prices.

Third, regional price convergence may instead be overstated because anticipatory solar investment makes the pre-integration price gap artificially large.

Empirical Setting

The Chilean electricity market provides two major transmission expansions.

The first is the 2017 interconnection between Antofagasta and Atacama.

The second is the 2019 reinforcement connecting Atacama more strongly with Santiago.

Atacama is a solar-intensive region, whereas Santiago is the country's main electricity demand center.

The empirical analysis combines hourly electricity prices, plant-level generation, generation costs, demand, plant characteristics, and transmission constraints.

Reduced-Form Generation-Cost Regression

Let ctc_tct​ denote observed nationwide generation cost per MWh. The authors construct ct∗c_t^*ct∗​ as the nationwide merit-order cost: the minimum generation cost that would be achievable if transmission constraints were absent, given contemporaneous demand, generation costs, and available capacity.

The estimating equation is

ct=β1It+β2Rt+β3Xt+θm+ut.(8.2.1.18)\boxed{ c_t = \beta_1 I_t + \beta_2 R_t + \beta_3 X_t + \theta_m + u_t }. \tag{8.2.1.18}ct​=β1​It​+β2​Rt​+β3​Xt​+θm​+ut​​.(8.2.1.18)

Here,

It=1[t≥2017 interconnection],(8.2.1.19)I_t = 1[ t\geq \text{2017 interconnection} ], \tag{8.2.1.19}It​=1[t≥2017 interconnection],(8.2.1.19)

and

Rt=1[t≥2019 reinforcement].(8.2.1.20)R_t = 1[ t\geq \text{2019 reinforcement} ]. \tag{8.2.1.20}Rt​=1[t≥2019 reinforcement].(8.2.1.20)

The vector XtX_tXt​ includes the nationwide merit-order cost ct∗c_t^*ct∗​ and additional fundamentals such as fuel prices, hydro availability, and demand. Month fixed effects control for seasonality. The coefficients β1,β2\beta_1,\beta_2β1​,β2​ measure changes in generation costs associated with the two transmission expansions, holding contemporaneous generation fundamentals fixed.

Reduced-Form Estimates

In the preferred specifications, the interconnection reduces generation cost at noon by approximately 2.42  USD/MWh2.42\;\text{USD/MWh}2.42USD/MWh, while the reinforcement produces an additional reduction of approximately 0.96 USD/MWh0.96\ \text{USD/MWh}0.96 USD/MWh. Using all hours, the corresponding estimates are approximately 2.07  USD/MWh2.07\;\text{USD/MWh}2.07USD/MWh and 0.62  USD/MWh0.62\;\text{USD/MWh}0.62USD/MWh. These estimates capture the change around the physical transmission expansions but do not capture solar investment that occurred beforehand in anticipation of integration.

Why a Structural Model Is Needed

The central counterfactual is: What solar capacity would have been built if market integration had never occurred? This quantity is not observed. A standard event study cannot recover it because solar investment had already responded before the transmission lines opened. The paper therefore combines

Short-Run Dispatch Model+Long-Run Investment Model(8.2.1.21)\boxed{\text{Short-Run Dispatch Model}+\text{Long-Run Investment Model}} \tag{8.2.1.21}Short-Run Dispatch Model+Long-Run Investment Model​(8.2.1.21)

Short-Run Dispatch Model

Index geographic zones by zzz, hours by ttt, technologies by jjj, and transmission lines by lll. The system operator chooses generation, imports, and exports to minimize total generation cost:

min⁡q,imp,exp∑z,t,jCztj(qztj)(8.2.1.22)\boxed{\min_{q,imp,exp}\sum_{z,t,j}C_{ztj}(q_{ztj})} \tag{8.2.1.22}q,imp,expmin​z,t,j∑​Cztj​(qztj​)​(8.2.1.22)

The main supply-demand constraint is

∑jqztj+∑l[(1−δ1)implzt−explzt]≥Dzt1−δ2.(8.2.1.23)\sum_j q_{ztj}+\sum_l\left[(1-\delta_1)imp_{lzt}-exp_{lzt}\right]\geq\frac{D_{zt}}{1-\delta_2}. \tag{8.2.1.23}j∑​qztj​+l∑​[(1−δ1​)implzt​−explzt​]≥1−δ2​Dzt​​.(8.2.1.23)

Transmission flows are restricted by line capacity:

0≤implzt≤flz,(8.2.1.24)0\leq imp_{lzt} \leq f_{lz}, \tag{8.2.1.24}0≤implzt​≤flz​,(8.2.1.24)

and

0≤explzt≤flz.(8.2.1.25)0\leq exp_{lzt}\leq f_{lz}. \tag{8.2.1.25}0≤explzt​≤flz​.(8.2.1.25)

Flows must also balance across connected regions:

∑z(implzt−explzt)=0(8.2.1.26)\sum_z\left(imp_{lzt}-exp_{lzt}\right)=0 \tag{8.2.1.26}z∑​(implzt​−explzt​)=0(8.2.1.26)

The remaining technology-specific constraints are omitted here because they are not central to the investment mechanism. The solution generates equilibrium hourly production and local electricity prices:

(k,f,Demand,Costs)→{qztj,pzt}(8.2.1.27)(k,f,\text{Demand},\text{Costs})\rightarrow\left\{q_{ztj},p_{zt}\right\} \tag{8.2.1.27}(k,f,Demand,Costs)→{qztj​,pzt​}(8.2.1.27)

Solar Investment Model

Let kzk_zkz​ denote installed solar capacity in zone zzz. Solar entry is assumed to be competitive. Investors expand capacity until the expected present value of solar revenues equals the investment cost:

E[∑y∈Y∑hpzyh(k)qzyh(k)(1+r)y]=czkz∀z.(8.2.1.28)\boxed{ E \left[ \sum_{y\in Y} \sum_h \frac{ p_{zyh}(k) q_{zyh}(k) }{ (1+r)^y } \right] = c_z k_z \qquad \forall z }. \tag{8.2.1.28}E​y∈Y∑​h∑​(1+r)ypzyh​(k)qzyh​(k)​​=cz​kz​∀z​.(8.2.1.28)

where pzyh(k)p_{zyh}(k)pzyh​(k) is the equilibrium electricity price implied by the dispatch model, qzyh(k)q_{zyh}(k)qzyh​(k) is solar generation, rrr is the discount rate, and czc_zcz​ is investment cost per MW of solar capacity.

Because additional solar capacity depresses local electricity prices, we have:

kz↑→pzyh(k)↓.(8.2.1.29)k_z\uparrow \rightarrow p_{zyh}(k)\downarrow. \tag{8.2.1.29}kz​↑→pzyh​(k)↓.(8.2.1.29)

Therefore the marginal profitability of solar investment decreases with installed capacity. This “cannibalization” effect generates a finite free-entry equilibrium.

Investment Equilibrium

The equilibrium solar capacity kz∗k_z^*kz∗​ solves:

NPV Revenuez(k∗)=Investment Costz(kz∗).(8.2.1.30)\text{NPV Revenue}_z(k^*)=\text{Investment Cost}_z(k_z^*). \tag{8.2.1.30}NPV Revenuez​(k∗)=Investment Costz​(kz∗​).(8.2.1.30)

Equivalently,

Πz(k∗)=0.(8.2.1.31)\Pi_z(k^*)=0. \tag{8.2.1.31}Πz​(k∗)=0.(8.2.1.31)

The structural equilibrium therefore solves the fixed-point problem

k→Dispatch→[p(k),q(k)]→Investment Profitability→k∗(8.2.1.32)k\rightarrow\text{Dispatch}\rightarrow\left[p(k),q(k)\right]\rightarrow\text{Investment Profitability} \rightarrow k^* \tag{8.2.1.32}k→Dispatch→[p(k),q(k)]→Investment Profitability→k∗(8.2.1.32)

Estimation of Solar Investment Costs

The observed solar capacity under the actual transmission network is treated as an equilibrium outcome. Given observed kzk_zkz​, the authors first solve the dispatch model to obtain pzyh(kz)p_{zyh}(k_z)pzyh​(kz​) and qzyh(kz)q_{zyh}(k_z)qzyh​(kz​). These objects are inserted into the zero-profit condition.

The discount rate is r=0.0583r=0.0583r=0.0583, and the assumed lifetime of a solar installation is 25 years. The zero-profit condition then identifies the implied investment cost per MW:

cz=E[∑y,hpzyh(k)qzyh(k)(1+r)y]kz.(8.2.1.33)c_z = \frac{ E \left[ \sum_{y,h} \dfrac{ p_{zyh}(k) q_{zyh}(k) }{ (1+r)^y } \right] }{ k_z }. \tag{8.2.1.33}cz​=kz​E[∑y,h​(1+r)ypzyh​(k)qzyh​(k)​]​.(8.2.1.33)

For the two main solar regions, the estimated costs are approximately c1=1.84 million USD/MWc_1=1.84\text{ million USD/MW}c1​=1.84 million USD/MW and c2=1.67 million USD/MWc_2=1.67\text{ million USD/MW}c2​=1.67 million USD/MW. These estimates are broadly consistent with observed solar installation costs.

Counterfactual Investment

Once czc_zcz​ has been recovered, the authors change transmission capacities

flz(8.2.1.34)f_{lz} \tag{8.2.1.34}flz​(8.2.1.34)

to represent alternative market-integration scenarios.

For any candidate capacity kzk_zkz​, the dispatch model produces

pzyh(k)andqzyh(k).(8.2.1.35)p_{zyh}(k) \qquad\text{and}\qquad q_{zyh}(k). \tag{8.2.1.35}pzyh​(k)andqzyh​(k).(8.2.1.35)

The authors then search for

kz∗(8.2.1.36)k_z^* \tag{8.2.1.36}kz∗​(8.2.1.36)

that simultaneously satisfies the dispatch equilibrium and the zero-profit condition.

Schematically,

f→p(k;f),q(k;f)→Π(k;f)→k∗(f).(8.2.1.37)f \rightarrow p(k;f),q(k;f) \rightarrow \Pi(k;f) \rightarrow k^*(f). \tag{8.2.1.37}f→p(k;f),q(k;f)→Π(k;f)→k∗(f).(8.2.1.37)

Thus changing transmission capacity changes both short-run dispatch and long-run generation investment.

Three Counterfactual Scenarios

The paper compares three equilibrium environments.

The first is the actual integrated market:

Scenario 1=Market Integration+Observed Investment.(8.2.1.38)\text{Scenario 1} = \text{Market Integration} + \text{Observed Investment}. \tag{8.2.1.38}Scenario 1=Market Integration+Observed Investment.(8.2.1.38)

The second removes market integration but holds solar capacity fixed:

Scenario 2=No Market Integration+Fixed Investment.(8.2.1.39)\text{Scenario 2}=\text{No Market Integration}+\text{Fixed Investment}. \tag{8.2.1.39}Scenario 2=No Market Integration+Fixed Investment.(8.2.1.39)

The comparison Scenario 1−Scenario 2\text{Scenario 1}-\text{Scenario 2}Scenario 1−Scenario 2 isolates the conventional gains-from-trade effect.

The third removes market integration and allows investment to adjust:

Scenario 3=No Market Integration+Endogenous Investment.(8.2.1.40)\text{Scenario 3}=\text{No Market Integration}+\text{Endogenous Investment}. \tag{8.2.1.40}Scenario 3=No Market Integration+Endogenous Investment.(8.2.1.40)

The comparison

Scenario 1−Scenario 3(8.2.1.41)\boxed{ \text{Scenario 1} - \text{Scenario 3} } \tag{8.2.1.41}Scenario 1−Scenario 3​(8.2.1.41)

captures the full long-run effect of market integration, including induced renewable investment.

Counterfactual Solar Investment

Without market integration, equilibrium solar capacity would fall sharply.

For Antofagasta,

k1NoIntegration≈0.20k1Actual.(8.2.1.42)k_1^{NoIntegration} \approx 0.20 k_1^{Actual}. \tag{8.2.1.42}k1NoIntegration​≈0.20k1Actual​.(8.2.1.42)

For Atacama,

k2NoIntegration≈0.17k2Actual.(8.2.1.43)k_2^{NoIntegration} \approx 0.17 k_2^{Actual}. \tag{8.2.1.43}k2NoIntegration​≈0.17k2Actual​.(8.2.1.43)

Hence most of the observed solar capacity in these regions would not have been profitable without transmission expansion.

Main Quantitative Results

If solar investment is held fixed, market integration raises solar generation by only

10%.(8.2.1.44)10\%. \tag{8.2.1.44}10%.(8.2.1.44)

When endogenous investment is incorporated, the effect becomes

178%.(8.2.1.45)\boxed{ 178\% }. \tag{8.2.1.45}178%​.(8.2.1.45)

Similarly, the average generation-cost reduction is

−3%(8.2.1.46)-3\% \tag{8.2.1.46}−3%(8.2.1.46)

when investment is held fixed, compared with

−8%(8.2.1.47)\boxed{ -8\% } \tag{8.2.1.47}−8%​(8.2.1.47)

when investment effects are incorporated.

At noon, when solar generation is particularly important, the corresponding cost reductions are

−7%(8.2.1.48)-7\% \tag{8.2.1.48}−7%(8.2.1.48)

and

−18%.(8.2.1.49)\boxed{ -18\% }. \tag{8.2.1.49}−18%​.(8.2.1.49)

Price-Convergence Counterfactual

Holding solar investment fixed, the no-integration counterfactual generates a very low Atacama price because excessive solar capacity cannot export electricity.

The implied Santiago–Atacama price gap is

54 USD/MWh.(8.2.1.50)54\ \text{USD/MWh}. \tag{8.2.1.50}54 USD/MWh.(8.2.1.50)

The actual integrated-market gap is

6.4 USD/MWh.(8.2.1.51)6.4\ \text{USD/MWh}. \tag{8.2.1.51}6.4 USD/MWh.(8.2.1.51)

Ignoring investment responses would therefore imply price convergence of

54−6.4=47.6 USD/MWh.(8.2.1.52)54-6.4 = 47.6\ \text{USD/MWh}. \tag{8.2.1.52}54−6.4=47.6 USD/MWh.(8.2.1.52)

Once solar investment is allowed to adjust, the counterfactual no-integration price gap is only

14.4 USD/MWh.(8.2.1.53)14.4\ \text{USD/MWh}. \tag{8.2.1.53}14.4 USD/MWh.(8.2.1.53)

Hence the long-run price-convergence effect becomes

14.4−6.4=8 USD/MWh.(8.2.1.54)\boxed{ 14.4-6.4 = 8\ \text{USD/MWh} }. \tag{8.2.1.54}14.4−6.4=8 USD/MWh​.(8.2.1.54)

Thus ignoring endogenous investment can substantially overstate the effect of integration on spatial price convergence.

Identification Logic

The structural estimation relies on the following sequence:

Observed Solar Capacity+Observed Transmission Network(8.2.1.55)\text{Observed Solar Capacity} + \text{Observed Transmission Network} \tag{8.2.1.55}Observed Solar Capacity+Observed Transmission Network(8.2.1.55)
→Dispatch Model→p(k),q(k)(8.2.1.56)\rightarrow \text{Dispatch Model} \rightarrow p(k),q(k) \tag{8.2.1.56}→Dispatch Model→p(k),q(k)(8.2.1.56)
→Zero-Profit Condition→c^z.(8.2.1.57)\rightarrow \text{Zero-Profit Condition} \rightarrow \widehat c_z. \tag{8.2.1.57}→Zero-Profit Condition→cz​.(8.2.1.57)

After recovering investment costs,

c^z+Counterfactual Transmission Network(8.2.1.58)\widehat c_z + \text{Counterfactual Transmission Network} \tag{8.2.1.58}cz​+Counterfactual Transmission Network(8.2.1.58)
→Dispatch Equilibrium+Investment Equilibrium(8.2.1.59)\rightarrow \text{Dispatch Equilibrium} + \text{Investment Equilibrium} \tag{8.2.1.59}→Dispatch Equilibrium+Investment Equilibrium(8.2.1.59)
→kzCF,pCF,qCF,CostCF.(8.2.1.60)\rightarrow k_z^{CF}, \quad p^{CF}, \quad q^{CF}, \quad Cost^{CF}. \tag{8.2.1.60}→kzCF​,pCF,qCF,CostCF.(8.2.1.60)

Core Logic of the Paper

The entire empirical strategy can be summarized as

Transmission Expansion→Relaxed Spatial Constraints→Higher Export Opportunities(8.2.1.61)\text{Transmission Expansion} \rightarrow \text{Relaxed Spatial Constraints} \rightarrow \text{Higher Export Opportunities} \tag{8.2.1.61}Transmission Expansion→Relaxed Spatial Constraints→Higher Export Opportunities(8.2.1.61)
→Higher Expected Renewable Revenue→Renewable Entry(8.2.1.62)\rightarrow \text{Higher Expected Renewable Revenue} \rightarrow \text{Renewable Entry} \tag{8.2.1.62}→Higher Expected Renewable Revenue→Renewable Entry(8.2.1.62)
→More Low-Marginal-Cost Generation→Lower System Costs and Emissions.(8.2.1.63)\rightarrow \text{More Low-Marginal-Cost Generation} \rightarrow \text{Lower System Costs and Emissions}. \tag{8.2.1.63}→More Low-Marginal-Cost Generation→Lower System Costs and Emissions.(8.2.1.63)

The key methodological insight is

Observed Before–After Effect≠Full Long-Run Policy Effect(8.2.1.64)\boxed{ \text{Observed Before--After Effect} \neq \text{Full Long-Run Policy Effect} } \tag{8.2.1.64}Observed Before–After Effect=Full Long-Run Policy Effect​(8.2.1.64)

when firms can anticipate future market integration.

The full effect must compare two long-run equilibria:

Integrated Market with Endogenous Investmentvs.Separated Market with Endogenous Investment.(8.2.1.65)\boxed{ \text{Integrated Market with Endogenous Investment} \quad\text{vs.}\quad \text{Separated Market with Endogenous Investment}. } \tag{8.2.1.65}Integrated Market with Endogenous Investmentvs.Separated Market with Endogenous Investment.​(8.2.1.65)

References

  • Gonzales, Luis E, Koichiro Ito, and Mar Reguant. 2023. “The investment effects of market integration: Evidence from renewable energy expansion in Chile.” Econometrica, 91(5): 1659–1693.

This schematic line is the research question written as a decomposition, not an equation to be solved. The left side is the policy: connecting previously separated electricity markets with transmission lines. The right side splits the total effect into two conceptually different pieces.

The first piece, gains from trade, holds the set of power plants fixed and asks how much cheaper it becomes to serve demand when production can be moved to the lowest-cost plants wherever they are located. In the stylized model this is the move from the autarky allocation in equation (3) to the integrated allocation in equation (5). The second piece, the investment effect, lets the capital stock respond: once a solar-rich region can export, solar entry becomes profitable and capacity grows, which is the move from equation (5) to equations (7)-(9).

In terms of the structural counterfactuals defined later, the decomposition can be written as

S1−S3⏟total effect=S1−S2⏟gains from trade+S2−S3⏟investment effect,\underbrace{S_1-S_3}_{\text{total effect}}=\underbrace{S_1-S_2}_{\text{gains from trade}}+\underbrace{S_2-S_3}_{\text{investment effect}},total effectS1​−S3​​​=gains from tradeS1​−S2​​​+investment effectS2​−S3​​​,

where S1,S2,S3S_1,S_2,S_3S1​,S2​,S3​ denote an outcome (cost, solar output, price gap) under Scenarios 1, 2 and 3 of equations (38)-(40). The “plus” sign is therefore an accounting identity once the three scenarios are defined; the substantive claim of the paper is that the second term is large and is missed by event studies when investment is anticipatory.

This is the assumed technology of the stylized model. Despite the letter CCC, the note states that these are marginal generation costs: Cr(qr)C_r(q_r)Cr​(qr​) is the cost of the last MWh produced by nonsolar plants in region rrr when they produce qrq_rqr​, measured in USD/MWh, and βr>0\beta_r>0βr​>0 is the slope of the regional supply curve. It is an upward-sloping merit order through the origin: plants are dispatched from cheapest to most expensive, and the marginal plant becomes more expensive as output grows.

The implied total variable cost is the area under the marginal cost curve,

TCr(qr)=∫0qrβrx dx=12βrqr2,TC_r(q_r)=\int_0^{q_r}\beta_r x\,dx=\tfrac{1}{2}\beta_r q_r^2,TCr​(qr​)=∫0qr​​βr​xdx=21​βr​qr2​,

which is strictly convex, so the cost-minimization problem behind equation (4) has a unique interior solution. Under competitive (or regulated cost-based) dispatch, price equals marginal cost, so Cr(qr)C_r(q_r)Cr​(qr​) is also the inverse supply curve; this is what delivers the autarky prices in equation (3).

The assumption βA≤βB\beta_A\leq\beta_BβA​≤βB​ says that at equal output region AAA is cheaper at the margin. Linearity through the origin buys closed forms for every object that follows (equations (5), (9), (15)); it rules out capacity limits, fixed costs and steps in the merit order, all of which are restored in the full dispatch model of equations (22)-(26).

Start from the two primitives of the autarky case: there is no transmission, so each region must serve its own (perfectly inelastic) demand with its own nonsolar plants, and price equals the marginal cost of the last unit dispatched, given by equation (2).

Step 1 (market clearing region by region). With no line and no solar,

qA=DA,qB=DB.q_A=D_A,\qquad q_B=D_B .qA​=DA​,qB​=DB​.

Step 2 (marginal-cost pricing). Insert these quantities in the marginal cost functions of equation (2):

pA=CA(DA)=βADA,pB=CB(DB)=βBDB.p_A=C_A(D_A)=\beta_A D_A,\qquad p_B=C_B(D_B)=\beta_B D_B .pA​=CA​(DA​)=βA​DA​,pB​=CB​(DB​)=βB​DB​.

This is the target. The note then restricts attention to pA<pBp_A<p_BpA​<pB​, that is βADA<βBDB\beta_A D_A<\beta_B D_BβA​DA​<βB​DB​, which is the condition under which region AAA would export if a line existed. For later use, the total variable cost of serving demand under autarky is the sum of the two areas under the marginal cost curves,

TCaut=12βADA2+12βBDB2.TC^{\text{aut}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\beta_A D_A^2+\tfrac{1}{2}\beta_B D_B^2 .TCaut=21​βA​DA2​+21​βB​DB2​.

As a running numerical example take βA=1\beta_A=1βA​=1, βB=2\beta_B=2βB​=2 and DA=DB=30D_A=D_B=30DA​=DB​=30; then pA=30p_A=30pA​=30, pB=60p_B=60pB​=60 and TCaut=1350TC^{\text{aut}}=1350TCaut=1350.

Under full integration a planner (or a competitive market with an unconstrained line) serves total demand D=DA+DBD=D_A+D_BD=DA​+DB​ at least cost. Using the total cost functions implied by equation (2), the problem is

min⁡qA,qB 12βAqA2+12βBqB2s.t.qA+qB=D.\min_{q_A,q_B}\ \tfrac{1}{2}\beta_A q_A^2+\tfrac{1}{2}\beta_B q_B^2\quad\text{s.t.}\quad q_A+q_B=D .qA​,qB​min​ 21​βA​qA2​+21​βB​qB2​s.t.qA​+qB​=D.

Step 1. Form the Lagrangian with multiplier λ\lambdaλ on the adding-up constraint:

L=12βAqA2+12βBqB2+λ (D−qA−qB).\mathcal{L}=\tfrac{1}{2}\beta_A q_A^2+\tfrac{1}{2}\beta_B q_B^2+\lambda\,(D-q_A-q_B).L=21​βA​qA2​+21​βB​qB2​+λ(D−qA​−qB​).

Step 2. The first-order conditions with respect to qAq_AqA​ and qBq_BqB​ are

βAqA−λ=0,βBqB−λ=0.\beta_A q_A-\lambda=0,\qquad \beta_B q_B-\lambda=0 .βA​qA​−λ=0,βB​qB​−λ=0.

Step 3. The multiplier λ\lambdaλ is the cost of serving one more MWh of demand anywhere in the integrated system, which is the common market price; call it p∗p^*p∗. Combining the two first-order conditions with the constraint gives

βAqA=βBqB=p∗,qA+qB=D,\beta_A q_A=\beta_B q_B=p^*,\qquad q_A+q_B=D ,βA​qA​=βB​qB​=p∗,qA​+qB​=D,

which is the target. Because the objective is strictly convex and the constraint is linear, these conditions are sufficient as well as necessary. Economically: if marginal costs differed, moving one MWh from the high-marginal-cost region to the low one would reduce total cost, so equalization of marginal costs is exactly the absence of unexploited gains from trade.

Solve the three equations in equation (4) for the three unknowns qAq_AqA​, qBq_BqB​ and p∗p^*p∗.

Step 1. Invert the two marginal-cost conditions to express quantities as functions of the price:

qA=p∗βA,qB=p∗βB.q_A=\frac{p^*}{\beta_A},\qquad q_B=\frac{p^*}{\beta_B}.qA​=βA​p∗​,qB​=βB​p∗​.

Step 2. Substitute in the adding-up constraint and solve for the price:

D=p∗βA+p∗βB=p∗ βA+βBβAβB⟹p∗=βAβBβA+βB D.\begin{aligned} D&=\frac{p^*}{\beta_A}+\frac{p^*}{\beta_B}=p^*\,\frac{\beta_A+\beta_B}{\beta_A\beta_B}\\ \Longrightarrow\quad p^*&=\frac{\beta_A\beta_B}{\beta_A+\beta_B}\,D . \end{aligned}D⟹p∗​=βA​p∗​+βB​p∗​=p∗βA​βB​βA​+βB​​=βA​+βB​βA​βB​​D.​

Step 3. Put the price back in Step 1:

qA=βBβA+βBD,qB=βAβA+βBD.q_A=\frac{\beta_B}{\beta_A+\beta_B}D,\qquad q_B=\frac{\beta_A}{\beta_A+\beta_B}D .qA​=βA​+βB​βB​​D,qB​=βA​+βB​βA​​D.

Step 4 (where the integrated price lies). Write p∗p^*p∗ as a weighted average of the autarky prices of equation (3):

p∗=βBβA+βB βADA+βAβA+βB βBDB=βBβA+βB pA+βAβA+βB pB,p^*=\frac{\beta_B}{\beta_A+\beta_B}\,\beta_A D_A+\frac{\beta_A}{\beta_A+\beta_B}\,\beta_B D_B=\frac{\beta_B}{\beta_A+\beta_B}\,p_A+\frac{\beta_A}{\beta_A+\beta_B}\,p_B ,p∗=βA​+βB​βB​​βA​DA​+βA​+βB​βA​​βB​DB​=βA​+βB​βB​​pA​+βA​+βB​βA​​pB​,

so pA<p∗<pBp_A<p^*<p_BpA​<p∗<pB​ whenever pA<pBp_A<p_BpA​<pB​: the price rises in the exporting region and falls in the importing region. Region AAA exports qA−DA=(pB−pA)/(βA+βB)>0q_A-D_A=(p_B-p_A)/(\beta_A+\beta_B)>0qA​−DA​=(pB​−pA​)/(βA​+βB​)>0.

In the running example (βA=1\beta_A=1βA​=1, βB=2\beta_B=2βB​=2, DA=DB=30D_A=D_B=30DA​=DB​=30): p∗=40p^*=40p∗=40, qA=40q_A=40qA​=40, qB=20q_B=20qB​=20, and region AAA exports 101010.

This arrow diagram names the conventional, short-run channel: with a fixed fleet of plants, a new line lets the operator replace expensive generation in the importing region with cheaper generation in the exporting region. Nothing is built; only the dispatch changes.

The size of this effect in the stylized model can be computed from equations (3) and (5). Total variable cost under autarky is 12βADA2+12βBDB2\tfrac{1}{2}\beta_A D_A^2+\tfrac{1}{2}\beta_B D_B^221​βA​DA2​+21​βB​DB2​, and under integration it is 12p∗D\tfrac{1}{2}p^*D21​p∗D. Their difference is

TCaut−TC∗=(βADA−βBDB)22(βA+βB)=(pB−pA)22(βA+βB) ≥0,TC^{\text{aut}}-TC^{*}=\frac{(\beta_A D_A-\beta_B D_B)^2}{2(\beta_A+\beta_B)}=\frac{(p_B-p_A)^2}{2(\beta_A+\beta_B)}\ \geq 0 ,TCaut−TC∗=2(βA​+βB​)(βA​DA​−βB​DB​)2​=2(βA​+βB​)(pB​−pA​)2​ ≥0,

the familiar Harberger triangle: half the autarky price gap times the trade volume (pB−pA)/(βA+βB)(p_B-p_A)/(\beta_A+\beta_B)(pB​−pA​)/(βA​+βB​). The gain is zero only if autarky prices already coincide and grows with the square of the price gap. In the running example it equals 1350−1200=1501350-1200=1501350−1200=150.

In the empirical part this channel corresponds to the comparison of Scenario 1 with Scenario 2 (equations (38)-(39)), where solar capacity is held at its observed level and only the network changes. The paper's point is that this is only part of the story, because the same line also changes which plants get built (equations (10)-(11)).

Now add solar, which can be built only in region AAA, has zero marginal cost, and needs a price of at least ccc per MWh to cover its investment cost. The markets are integrated.

Step 1 (free entry pins down the price). If the integrated price exceeded ccc, each additional unit of solar would earn positive profit and entry would continue, pushing out nonsolar generation and lowering the price. If the price were below ccc, no one would build. Since c<p∗c<p^*c<p∗, entry is positive at the no-solar price of equation (5) and stops exactly when

p∗∗=c.p^{**}=c .p∗∗=c.

Step 2 (nonsolar supply at that price). The nonsolar plants in both regions are still dispatched until their marginal cost, equation (2), equals the common price, exactly as in equation (4) but with p∗∗p^{**}p∗∗ in place of p∗p^*p∗:

βAqA=p∗∗=c,βBqB=p∗∗=c.\beta_A q_A=p^{**}=c,\qquad \beta_B q_B=p^{**}=c .βA​qA​=p∗∗=c,βB​qB​=p∗∗=c.

Step 3. Solving for quantities gives the target:

qA=cβA,qB=cβB.q_A=\frac{c}{\beta_A},\qquad q_B=\frac{c}{\beta_B}.qA​=βA​c​,qB​=βB​c​.

Both are lower than the quantities in equation (5) because c<p∗c<p^*c<p∗: solar displaces nonsolar generation in both regions in proportion to 1/βr1/\beta_r1/βr​, which is possible only because the line carries solar power from AAA to BBB. In the running example with c=36c=36c=36: qA=36q_A=36qA​=36 and qB=18q_B=18qB​=18, compared with 404040 and 202020 without solar.

This is the market-clearing condition of the integrated system with three sources of supply. Demand is perfectly inelastic at D=DA+DBD=D_A+D_BD=DA​+DB​ and the line is unconstrained, so there is a single energy balance:

qA+qB+qsolar=D.q_A+q_B+q_{\mathrm{solar}}=D .qA​+qB​+qsolar​=D.

The nonsolar quantities are not free: by equation (7) they are determined by the free-entry price ccc. Solar output is therefore the only variable left to close the balance, and rearranging gives

qsolar=D−qA−qB.q_{\mathrm{solar}}=D-q_A-q_B .qsolar​=D−qA​−qB​.

The logic is the reverse of the usual one. Normally quantity supplied determines the price; here free entry fixes the price at ccc, the price fixes nonsolar output, and solar capacity adjusts to fill whatever demand is left. In the stylized model there is one representative hour, so solar capacity and solar output are the same object; the full model separates them through hourly capacity factors (equation (28)).

Combine the residual-demand identity of equation (8) with the nonsolar quantities of equation (7).

Step 1. Substitute qA=c/βAq_A=c/\beta_AqA​=c/βA​ and qB=c/βBq_B=c/\beta_BqB​=c/βB​:

qsolar=D−cβA−cβB.q_{\mathrm{solar}}=D-\frac{c}{\beta_A}-\frac{c}{\beta_B}.qsolar​=D−βA​c​−βB​c​.

Step 2. Put the two fractions over a common denominator:

qsolar=D−βB+βAβAβB c,q_{\mathrm{solar}}=D-\frac{\beta_B+\beta_A}{\beta_A\beta_B}\,c ,qsolar​=D−βA​βB​βB​+βA​​c,

which is the boxed result.

Step 3 (sign and interpretation). Using equation (5), D=βA+βBβAβBp∗D=\frac{\beta_A+\beta_B}{\beta_A\beta_B}p^*D=βA​βB​βA​+βB​​p∗, so

qsolar=βA+βBβAβB (p∗−c),q_{\mathrm{solar}}=\frac{\beta_A+\beta_B}{\beta_A\beta_B}\,(p^*-c),qsolar​=βA​βB​βA​+βB​​(p∗−c),

which is positive exactly when c<p∗c<p^*c<p∗, the maintained assumption. Solar entry equals the horizontal distance, along the aggregate nonsolar supply curve with slope βAβB/(βA+βB)\beta_A\beta_B/(\beta_A+\beta_B)βA​βB​/(βA​+βB​), between the no-solar price p∗p^*p∗ and the entry price ccc. It is larger when solar is cheaper (low ccc), when demand is larger, and when nonsolar supply is flatter.

Under autarky the same logic gives zero entry: solar in AAA would face the price pA<cp_A<cpA​<c, so qsolar=0q_{\mathrm{solar}}=0qsolar​=0. The whole quantity in the box is therefore caused by integration. In the running example, qsolar=60−32⋅36=6q_{\mathrm{solar}}=60-\tfrac{3}{2}\cdot 36=6qsolar​=60−23​⋅36=6.

This is the first half of the causal chain for the investment effect (it continues in equation (11)). It is a verbal statement about the constraint set faced by a solar plant in the solar-rich region, not something to be derived.

Without a line, every MWh of solar produced in region AAA must be consumed in region AAA. A larger line capacity relaxes this constraint: solar output can also serve demand in region BBB. In the stylized model the relaxation is all-or-nothing (no line versus an unconstrained line). In the full dispatch model it is continuous: exports from zone zzz over line lll are bounded by the capacity flzf_{lz}flz​ in equations (24)-(25), and raising flzf_{lz}flz​ enlarges the feasible set of the cost-minimization problem in equation (22).

The relevant market size for a solar investor changes accordingly. Under autarky a plant in AAA faces local demand DAD_ADA​ and the steep local residual demand implied by βA\beta_AβA​ alone; under integration it faces D=DA+DBD=D_A+D_BD=DA​+DB​ and the flatter aggregate nonsolar supply curve with slope

βAβBβA+βB<βA,\frac{\beta_A\beta_B}{\beta_A+\beta_B}<\beta_A ,βA​+βB​βA​βB​​<βA​,

so each additional MWh of solar depresses the price it receives by less. This is why export capability is the prerequisite for the price and revenue effects in equation (11).

This line completes the chain started in equation (10). Each arrow can be read off the stylized model.

First arrow: integration raises the price in the exporting region. By equations (3) and (5), the price in AAA moves from pA=βADAp_A=\beta_A D_ApA​=βA​DA​ to p∗p^*p∗, and

p∗−pA=βAβA+βB (pB−pA)>0.p^*-p_A=\frac{\beta_A}{\beta_A+\beta_B}\,(p_B-p_A)>0 .p∗−pA​=βA​+βB​βA​​(pB​−pA​)>0.

Second arrow: solar has zero marginal cost, so its revenue per MWh is the local price; a higher price in AAA directly raises the expected revenue of a plant located there. Third arrow: under the assumption pA<c<p∗p_A<c<p^*pA​<c<p∗, the price in AAA crosses the entry threshold ccc, so investment that was unprofitable under autarky becomes profitable and entry proceeds until the price is driven back down to ccc, giving the capacity in equation (9).

Note the direction of the price change: integration raises the price in the solar region while lowering it in the demand center. The investment effect therefore operates through the exporting region's price, which is why the paper focuses on prices in Antofagasta and Atacama. In the structural model the same chain appears as the dependence of the zero-profit capacity on the network, k∗(f)k^*(f)k∗(f), in equation (37).

Consider the transition period: the line has been announced, investors have already installed the long-run solar quantity qsolarq_{\mathrm{solar}}qsolar​ of equation (9) in region AAA, but the line is not yet in service, so the two regions are still separate markets.

Step 1 (energy balance in region AAA alone). With no flow across regions, supply in AAA consists of local nonsolar generation and the installed solar output:

qA+qsolar=DA.q_A+q_{\mathrm{solar}}=D_A .qA​+qsolar​=DA​.

Step 2 (merit order). Solar has zero marginal cost, so it is dispatched first; nonsolar plants serve only what is left:

qA=DA−qsolar.q_A=D_A-q_{\mathrm{solar}} .qA​=DA​−qsolar​.

This is the target. Region BBB is unaffected in the transition, qB=DBq_B=D_BqB​=DB​ and pB=βBDBp_B=\beta_B D_BpB​=βB​DB​, because none of the solar power can reach it. The equation presumes that solar does not exceed local demand, qsolar≤DAq_{\mathrm{solar}}\leq D_Aqsolar​≤DA​; otherwise nonsolar output would hit zero, the surplus would be curtailed, and the local price would fall to zero. The note leaves this condition implicit. In the running example qA=30−6=24q_A=30-6=24qA​=30−6=24.

Substitute the long-run solar quantity from equation (9) into the transition-period balance of equation (12).

Step 1. Insert qsolar=D−βA+βBβAβBcq_{\mathrm{solar}}=D-\frac{\beta_A+\beta_B}{\beta_A\beta_B}cqsolar​=D−βA​βB​βA​+βB​​c:

qA=DA−(D−βA+βBβAβB c).q_A=D_A-\left(D-\frac{\beta_A+\beta_B}{\beta_A\beta_B}\,c\right).qA​=DA​−(D−βA​βB​βA​+βB​​c).

Step 2. Use D=DA+DBD=D_A+D_BD=DA​+DB​, so that DA−D=−DBD_A-D=-D_BDA​−D=−DB​:

qA=βA+βBβAβB c−DB.q_A=\frac{\beta_A+\beta_B}{\beta_A\beta_B}\,c-D_B .qA​=βA​βB​βA​+βB​​c−DB​.

This is the target. A useful reading: the first term is total nonsolar output in the long-run integrated equilibrium, c/βA+c/βBc/\beta_A+c/\beta_Bc/βA​+c/βB​ from equation (7). In the transition, region BBB still produces all of its own demand DBD_BDB​ at high cost, and region AAA's nonsolar plants produce only the remainder. Nonsolar output in AAA is non-negative only if

c ≥ βAβBβA+βB DB,c\ \geq\ \frac{\beta_A\beta_B}{\beta_A+\beta_B}\,D_B ,c ≥ βA​+βB​βA​βB​​DB​,

This inequality is the identification problem of the paper in one line. An event study (or any before-after design) uses the outcome observed just before the line opens as the stand-in for what would have happened without the line. That is valid only if agents did not act on the policy before it took effect.

Here they did. Transmission lines take years to plan and build, so the opening date is known in advance, and solar plants were built in time for it. The pre-period therefore contains part of the treatment. In the stylized model the three relevant states are

(pA, qsolar=0)⏟no-policy counterfactual(p~A, qsolar>0)⏟observed pre-period(c, qsolar>0)⏟post-period\underbrace{(p_A,\ q_{\mathrm{solar}}=0)}_{\text{no-policy counterfactual}}\qquad \underbrace{(\widetilde p_A,\ q_{\mathrm{solar}}>0)}_{\text{observed pre-period}}\qquad \underbrace{(c,\ q_{\mathrm{solar}}>0)}_{\text{post-period}}no-policy counterfactual(pA​, qsolar​=0)​​observed pre-period(p​A​, qsolar​>0)​​post-period(c, qsolar​>0)​​

with the autarky price from equation (3), the transition price from equation (15) and the solar quantity from equation (9). A before-after comparison measures the distance between the second and third states, whereas the policy effect is the distance between the first and third.

The first state is never observed in the data, since by the time the line opens solar has already entered. This is what motivates the structural model: Scenario 3 in equation (40) is the model-based reconstruction of that unobserved state, and equation (17) and the price-gap calculation in equations (50)-(54) quantify the resulting biases.

This is the reduced-form estimating equation, a time-series regression on Chilean system data. The dependent variable ctc_tct​ is the observed nationwide generation cost per MWh in period ttt (USD/MWh). ItI_tIt​ and RtR_tRt​ are the step dummies of equations (19) and (20), XtX_tXt​ is a vector of contemporaneous fundamentals, θm\theta_mθm​ are month-of-year fixed effects absorbing seasonality, and utu_tut​ is the error. The coefficients β1,β2,β3\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3β1​,β2​,β3​ here are regression coefficients and are unrelated to the cost slopes βA,βB\beta_A,\beta_BβA​,βB​ of the stylized model.

The key control inside XtX_tXt​ is the nationwide merit-order cost ct∗c_t^*ct∗​: the least cost of serving demand in period ttt if there were no transmission constraints, given that period's demand, plant costs and available capacity (including the solar capacity already installed). Since ct≥ct∗c_t\geq c_t^*ct​≥ct∗​ by construction, conditioning on ct∗c_t^*ct∗​ means the regression is effectively about the wedge

ct−ct∗ ≥0,c_t-c_t^*\ \geq 0 ,ct​−ct∗​ ≥0,

the cost of spatial misallocation caused by congestion. β1\beta_1β1​ is the change in this wedge after the 2017 interconnection, and β2\beta_2β2​ the additional change after the 2019 reinforcement; both are expected to be negative. Identification comes from comparing periods before and after each opening with the same fundamentals, under the assumption that no other shock to dispatch efficiency coincides with the openings.

The note reports about −2.42-2.42−2.42 and −0.96-0.96−0.96 USD/MWh at noon and −2.07-2.07−2.07 and −0.62-0.62−0.62 using all hours. Because ct∗c_t^*ct∗​ already embodies the solar plants built in anticipation, these coefficients measure the gains-from-trade channel of equation (6) and miss the investment effect, which is the bias described in equation (17).

ItI_tIt​ is the treatment indicator for the first transmission event: it equals one in every period on or after the date in 2017 when the interconnection between the two previously separate Chilean systems (the northern system around Antofagasta and the central system starting at Atacama) entered service, and zero before. The bracket notation 1[⋅]1[\cdot]1[⋅] is the indicator function.

Because ItI_tIt​ is a step function that stays at one, its coefficient β1\beta_1β1​ in equation (18) is a level shift in generation cost that persists after the opening, not a temporary effect. Written out,

E[ct∣It=1,Rt=0,Xt,m]−E[ct∣It=0,Rt=0,Xt,m]=β1.E[c_t\mid I_t=1,R_t=0,X_t,m]-E[c_t\mid I_t=0,R_t=0,X_t,m]=\beta_1 .E[ct​∣It​=1,Rt​=0,Xt​,m]−E[ct​∣It​=0,Rt​=0,Xt​,m]=β1​.

The dummy is switched on at the physical opening date, not at the announcement date. This choice is exactly what makes the regression a measure of the short-run reallocation effect only: investment responses that occurred between announcement and opening are already present when It=0I_t=0It​=0, as the stylized model shows in equations (12)-(15). The variation identifying β1\beta_1β1​ is purely time-series (one national series, one switching date), so the controls XtX_tXt​ and the month effects θm\theta_mθm​ carry the burden of making pre- and post-periods comparable.

RtR_tRt​ is the indicator for the second transmission event: it equals one on or after the date in 2019 when the reinforcement line strengthening the link between Atacama and the Santiago area entered service, and zero before. Since the reinforcement comes after the interconnection, the two dummies are nested: there are three regimes,

(It,Rt)=(0,0) before 2017,(1,0) between the two openings,(1,1) after 2019.(I_t,R_t)=(0,0)\ \text{before 2017},\qquad (1,0)\ \text{between the two openings},\qquad (1,1)\ \text{after 2019}.(It​,Rt​)=(0,0) before 2017,(1,0) between the two openings,(1,1) after 2019.

Consequently β2\beta_2β2​ in equation (18) is the incremental change in generation cost from the reinforcement relative to the interconnection-only regime, and the total change relative to the fully separated regime is β1+β2\beta_1+\beta_2β1​+β2​. With the note's noon estimates this total is about −2.42−0.96=−3.38-2.42-0.96=-3.38−2.42−0.96=−3.38 USD/MWh, and using all hours about −2.07−0.62=−2.69-2.07-0.62=-2.69−2.07−0.62=−2.69 USD/MWh.

The economic reason for separating the two events is that the 2017 interconnection alone left a bottleneck between the solar-rich north and the demand center; only the reinforcement let northern solar reach Santiago at scale. The same caveat as for equation (19) applies: the dummy switches at the physical opening, so solar capacity built in anticipation of the reinforcement is already in the data when Rt=0R_t=0Rt​=0.

This boxed line states the architecture of the structural model: two nested blocks, each answering a question the other cannot.

The short-run dispatch model (equations (22)-(27)) takes the capital stock as given, namely solar capacity kkk, other plants and the transmission network fff, and computes how the system operator would run that system hour by hour at least cost. Its outputs are generation by plant type and zonal prices. It is the empirical counterpart of equations (3)-(5) of the stylized model, with many zones, many technologies, line limits and losses.

The long-run investment model (equations (28)-(32)) takes the dispatch outcomes as given functions of kkk and determines kkk itself through free entry, the counterpart of the condition p∗∗=cp^{**}=cp∗∗=c behind equation (7).

The “plus” means composition, not addition: the investment model calls the dispatch model as an inner routine,

Πz(k;f)=NPV revenuez(p(k;f),q(k;f))−czkz,\Pi_z(k;f)=\text{NPV revenue}_z\big(p(k;f),q(k;f)\big)-c_z k_z ,Πz​(k;f)=NPV revenuez​(p(k;f),q(k;f))−cz​kz​,

and equilibrium capacity is the kkk at which this is zero in every solar zone. The combination is what allows the paper to construct the unobserved state of equation (16), a separated market in which investors never expected integration, which neither block could deliver alone: dispatch alone would keep the observed, anticipation-contaminated capacity, and an investment model without dispatch would have no prices to evaluate revenue.

This is the objective of the dispatch problem. The system operator chooses, for every zone zzz, hour ttt and technology jjj, the generation level qztjq_{ztj}qztj​, together with imports implztimp_{lzt}implzt​ and exports explztexp_{lzt}explzt​ on every line lll, to minimize the total variable cost of generation. Cztj(⋅)C_{ztj}(\cdot)Cztj​(⋅) is the cost function of technology jjj in zone zzz and hour ttt; for thermal units it is essentially fuel cost times output, and for solar, wind and run-of-river hydro it is approximately zero. The minimization is subject to equations (23)-(26) and to technology-specific capacity limits that the note omits.

Cost minimization is the right behavioral model here because the Chilean market is a cost-based pool: generators do not submit strategic price bids; the operator dispatches plants in merit order using audited variable costs. There is thus no market-power block to estimate. With linear costs the problem is a linear program, and it generalizes the two-region planner problem behind equation (4):

min⁡qA,qB 12βAqA2+12βBqB2s.t.qA+qB=D.\min_{q_A,q_B}\ \tfrac{1}{2}\beta_A q_A^2+\tfrac{1}{2}\beta_B q_B^2\quad\text{s.t.}\quad q_A+q_B=D .qA​,qB​min​ 21​βA​qA2​+21​βB​qB2​s.t.qA​+qB​=D.

Since the sum over ttt is separable across hours once ramping-type constraints are ignored, the problem can be solved hour by hour. Prices are not chosen; they emerge as the shadow values of the balance constraint in equation (23), as summarized in equation (27).

This is the energy-balance (supply-demand) constraint for each zone zzz and hour ttt. The left side is the power available in the zone: local generation summed over technologies, plus net inflows summed over the lines connected to the zone. The right side is the power that must be made available to deliver final consumption DztD_{zt}Dzt​.

Two loss parameters appear. δ1\delta_1δ1​ is the transmission loss rate: of each MWh sent over a line, only the fraction 1−δ11-\delta_11−δ1​ arrives, so imports are scaled down while exports leave the zone at full value. δ2\delta_2δ2​ is the loss rate between the zonal node and final consumers, so the zone must have Dzt/(1−δ2)>DztD_{zt}/(1-\delta_2)>D_{zt}Dzt​/(1−δ2​)>Dzt​ available. The weak inequality allows free disposal (curtailment of surplus renewable output); it binds whenever the marginal unit has positive cost.

The multiplier on this constraint, say λzt≥0\lambda_{zt}\geq 0λzt​≥0, is the marginal cost of making one more MWh available in zone zzz, which is the zonal price pztp_{zt}pzt​ of equation (27). For a line carrying power from zone zzz to zone z′z'z′, the first-order condition with respect to the flow gives

(1−δ1) pz′t−pzt=μlt ≥0,(1-\delta_1)\,p_{z't}-p_{zt}=\mu_{lt}\ \geq 0 ,(1−δ1​)pz′t​−pzt​=μlt​ ≥0,

where μlt\mu_{lt}μlt​ is the multiplier on the line limit of equations (24)-(25). When the line is uncongested, μlt=0\mu_{lt}=0μlt​=0 and prices differ only by losses; when it is congested, the price gap exceeds the loss wedge. This is the multi-zone analogue of the equal-marginal-cost condition in equation (4) and the source of the price-convergence results in equations (50)-(54).

This constraint bounds the power that zone zzz can import over line lll in hour ttt. Imports are non-negative because the direction of flow is encoded by using two separate variables, implztimp_{lzt}implzt​ and explztexp_{lzt}explzt​ (equation (25)), rather than one signed flow; this is convenient because losses in equation (23) apply only to the receiving side. The upper bound flzf_{lz}flz​ is the thermal (or security-constrained) capacity of the line as seen from zone zzz, in MW.

The parameter flzf_{lz}flz​ is the policy variable of the paper. Market integration is represented entirely through it:

flz=0  (no line: autarky),0<flz<∞  (limited integration),flz→∞  (full integration).f_{lz}=0\ \ \text{(no line: autarky)},\qquad 0<f_{lz}<\infty\ \ \text{(limited integration)},\qquad f_{lz}\to\infty\ \ \text{(full integration)}.flz​=0  (no line: autarky),0<flz​<∞  (limited integration),flz​→∞  (full integration).

The stylized model compares only the two extremes (equation (3) versus equation (5)); the dispatch model handles the realistic middle case, in which the line is congested in some hours, typically around noon when solar output peaks, and slack in others.

When the bound binds, its multiplier is the congestion rent per MWh and drives a wedge between zonal prices, as shown under equation (23). The counterfactual scenarios in equations (38)-(40) are generated by setting flzf_{lz}flz​ on the 2017 and 2019 lines back to their pre-expansion values, which is the object singled out in equation (34).

This is the mirror image of equation (24) for exports: the power that zone zzz sends out over line lll in hour ttt is non-negative and cannot exceed the line capacity flzf_{lz}flz​. Together the two constraints say that the line can carry at most flzf_{lz}flz​ in either direction.

For the investment mechanism the export bound is the one that matters in the solar zones. Around noon a zone with installed solar capacity kzk_zkz​ has zero-marginal-cost output that may exceed local demand. The surplus can leave only through exports, so the amount of solar the zone can absorb at a positive price is roughly bounded by

solar outputzt ≤ Dzt1−δ2+∑lflz,\text{solar output}_{zt}\ \leq\ \frac{D_{zt}}{1-\delta_2}+\sum_l f_{lz},solar outputzt​ ≤ 1−δ2​Dzt​​+l∑​flz​,

obtained from equation (23) when all other local generation is shut down and all lines export at capacity. If solar output exceeds this, the excess is curtailed and the local price falls to zero. Raising flzf_{lz}flz​ pushes this ceiling up, which is the precise sense of “ability to export solar electricity” in equation (10).

At an optimum the operator never both imports and exports on the same line in the same hour, since with losses δ1>0\delta_1>0δ1​>0 that would simply waste energy; hence at most one of implztimp_{lzt}implzt​ and explztexp_{lzt}explzt​ is positive.

This is the flow-conservation constraint for each line lll and hour ttt: summing over the zones the line connects, total imports equal total exports. For a line between zones zzz and z′z'z′ it reads

implzt−explzt+implz′t−explz′t=0,imp_{lzt}-exp_{lzt}+imp_{lz't}-exp_{lz't}=0 ,implzt​−explzt​+implz′t​−explz′t​=0,

so that if zzz exports xxx MWh and imports nothing, then z′z'z′ imports exactly xxx and exports nothing. The constraint ties together the import and export variables that appear separately in the zonal balances of equation (23); without it a zone could “import” power that no other zone sends.

Note where losses enter. Flows are measured at the sending end and conserved along the line by this constraint; the loss is then applied at the receiving end through the factor 1−δ11-\delta_11−δ1​ in equation (23). Thus xxx MWh exported relieve the balance of the exporter by xxx but help the importer by only (1−δ1)x(1-\delta_1)x(1−δ1​)x.

The formulation is a transport (pipeline) model of the grid: flows are chosen freely subject to capacity, without the Kirchhoff voltage-law constraints of a full power-flow model. For Chile this is a mild simplification because the network is essentially a long north-south line with little looping. This radial structure is also why two specific lines, the 2017 interconnection and the 2019 reinforcement, govern integration between the solar north and Santiago.

This line summarizes the dispatch model as a mapping from primitives to outcomes. The inputs are the vector of solar capacities kkk, the vector of line capacities fff, hourly zonal demand, and plant costs and availabilities. The outputs are the cost-minimizing generation qztjq_{ztj}qztj​ of each technology and the zonal prices pztp_{zt}pzt​.

The quantities are the solution of the program in equations (22)-(26). The prices are not choice variables: pztp_{zt}pzt​ is the Lagrange multiplier on the balance constraint (23), that is

pzt=∂ TCmin⁡(k,f,⋅)∂(Dzt/(1−δ2)),p_{zt}=\frac{\partial\, TC^{\min}(k,f,\cdot)}{\partial\big(D_{zt}/(1-\delta_2)\big)} ,pzt​=∂(Dzt​/(1−δ2​))∂TCmin(k,f,⋅)​,

the increase in minimized system cost from having to make one more MWh available in zone zzz at hour ttt. This is the locational marginal price: it equals the marginal cost of the marginal local unit when the zone is not import- or export-constrained, and it is linked to neighbors' prices through the congestion condition under equation (23).

Two properties of the mapping drive everything later. First, pztp_{zt}pzt​ is weakly decreasing in local solar capacity kzk_zkz​ (equation (29)). Second, in solar zones during solar hours pztp_{zt}pzt​ is weakly increasing in export capacity fff. The paper validates the mapping by comparing simulated prices and costs with observed ones under the actual network before using it for the investment condition in equation (28) and the counterfactuals in equation (37).

The zero-profit condition follows from free entry of small, price-taking solar investors.

Step 1 (output per MW). Let azyha_{zyh}azyh​ be solar output per MW of capacity in zone zzz, year yyy, hour hhh (the capacity factor, net of any curtailment). Total solar generation in the zone is then proportional to capacity:

qzyh(k)=azyh kz.q_{zyh}(k)=a_{zyh}\,k_z .qzyh​(k)=azyh​kz​.

E[∑y∈Y∑hpzyh(k) azyh(1+r)y]=cz.E\left[\sum_{y\in Y}\sum_h\frac{p_{zyh}(k)\,a_{zyh}}{(1+r)^y}\right]=c_z .E​y∈Y∑​h∑​(1+r)ypzyh​(k)azyh​​​=cz​.

Step 4 (aggregate to the zone). Multiply both sides by kzk_zkz​ and use Step 1 to replace azyhkza_{zyh}k_zazyh​kz​ by qzyh(k)q_{zyh}(k)qzyh​(k):

E[∑y∈Y∑hpzyh(k) qzyh(k)(1+r)y]=czkz∀z,E\left[\sum_{y\in Y}\sum_h\frac{p_{zyh}(k)\,q_{zyh}(k)}{(1+r)^y}\right]=c_z k_z\qquad\forall z ,E​y∈Y∑​h∑​(1+r)ypzyh​(k)qzyh​(k)​​=cz​kz​∀z,

which is the boxed condition. It holds for every solar zone simultaneously, and each zone's prices depend on the whole vector kkk, so it is a system of equations.

Two remarks. The condition equates average revenue per MW with cost; this coincides with the marginal entrant's condition only because all plants in a zone are identical and atomistic, so no investor internalizes the price reduction it imposes on others. And it is the dynamic, multi-hour version of the stylized condition p∗∗=cp^{**}=cp∗∗=c used in equation (7): there, a single representative hour makes the entry price itself equal to ccc.

This is the comparative-static property that makes the free-entry equilibrium well defined: more solar capacity in zone zzz lowers the prices that solar earns there. It is a property of the dispatch model, not an extra assumption.

The mechanism is the merit-order effect. Solar has zero marginal cost, so extra solar output shifts the residual demand faced by thermal plants to the left and the marginal plant becomes a cheaper one. If the zone could not trade, the stylized model gives the slope directly, as in equation (14):

∂pA∂qsolar=−βA(isolated region),∂p∂qsolar=−βAβBβA+βB(integrated regions).\frac{\partial p_A}{\partial q_{\mathrm{solar}}}=-\beta_A\quad\text{(isolated region)},\qquad \frac{\partial p}{\partial q_{\mathrm{solar}}}=-\frac{\beta_A\beta_B}{\beta_A+\beta_B}\quad\text{(integrated regions)}.∂qsolar​∂pA​​=−βA​(isolated region),∂qsolar​∂p​=−βA​+βB​βA​βB​​(integrated regions).

The second slope is smaller in absolute value: integration spreads the extra output over a larger market, so prices fall more slowly with capacity. In the full model the effect is stronger still when export lines congest (equation (25)), because then the zone is effectively isolated at the margin, and at the extreme surplus solar is curtailed and the price is zero.

The effect is concentrated in the hours when solar actually produces, so the price that matters for revenue, the output-weighted average, falls faster than the simple average price. This cannibalization is why the left side of equation (28) per MW declines in kzk_zkz​ and crosses czc_zcz​ once, giving a finite kz∗k_z^*kz∗​. It is also why transmission matters so much for investment: it flattens this decline.

This is the equilibrium condition of equation (28) restated in words for the equilibrium capacity vector. The left side is the expected discounted revenue of all solar plants in zone zzz, and the right side is what it costs to build them:

NPV Revenuez(k∗)=E[∑y∈Y∑hpzyh(k∗) qzyh(k∗)(1+r)y],Investment Costz(kz∗)=czkz∗.\text{NPV Revenue}_z(k^*)=E\left[\sum_{y\in Y}\sum_h\frac{p_{zyh}(k^*)\,q_{zyh}(k^*)}{(1+r)^y}\right],\qquad \text{Investment Cost}_z(k_z^*)=c_z k_z^* .NPV Revenuez​(k∗)=E​y∈Y∑​h∑​(1+r)ypzyh​(k∗)qzyh​(k∗)​​,Investment Costz​(kz∗​)=cz​kz∗​.

The notation carries an asymmetry that matters. Revenue in zone zzz depends on the entire vector k∗k^*k∗, because prices in zone zzz are affected by solar built in neighboring zones whenever the zones are electrically connected: solar in Antofagasta competes with solar in Atacama for the same export corridor and the same Santiago demand. Investment cost depends only on the zone's own capacity kz∗k_z^*kz∗​ and is linear in it, meaning a constant cost per MW with no scarcity of sites, no learning and no scale effects.

The condition is therefore one equation per solar zone in as many unknowns, to be solved jointly. A higher czc_zcz​ shifts the cost line up and lowers kz∗k_z^*kz∗​; a larger line capacity shifts the revenue curve up in the exporting zones and raises kz∗k_z^*kz∗​. The equivalent zero-profit form is equation (31) and the algorithmic form is equation (32).

Define aggregate solar profit in zone zzz as discounted expected revenue minus investment cost, for any capacity vector kkk:

Πz(k)=E[∑y∈Y∑hpzyh(k) qzyh(k)(1+r)y]−czkz.\Pi_z(k)=E\left[\sum_{y\in Y}\sum_h\frac{p_{zyh}(k)\,q_{zyh}(k)}{(1+r)^y}\right]-c_z k_z .Πz​(k)=E​y∈Y∑​h∑​(1+r)ypzyh​(k)qzyh​(k)​​−cz​kz​.

Step 1. By equation (30) (equivalently, equation (28) evaluated at the equilibrium vector), the two terms on the right are equal at k=k∗k=k^*k=k∗.

Step 2. Subtracting one from the other gives

Πz(k∗)=NPV Revenuez(k∗)−czkz∗=0,\Pi_z(k^*)=\text{NPV Revenue}_z(k^*)-c_z k_z^*=0 ,Πz​(k∗)=NPV Revenuez​(k∗)−cz​kz∗​=0,

which is the target, holding for every zone with positive solar capacity.

Step 3 (the complete statement). Allowing for zones in which no solar is built, free entry is a complementarity condition:

Πz(k∗)≤0,kz∗≥0,kz∗ Πz(k∗)=0,\Pi_z(k^*)\leq 0,\qquad k_z^*\geq 0,\qquad k_z^*\,\Pi_z(k^*)=0 ,Πz​(k∗)≤0,kz∗​≥0,kz∗​Πz​(k∗)=0,

where for a zone with kz∗=0k_z^*=0kz∗​=0 the inequality is to be read per MW: the first MW would not cover its cost. The stylized model shows both cases. Under integration, entry is positive and the zero-profit price is p∗∗=cp^{**}=cp∗∗=c (equation (7)); under autarky, the price pA<cp_A<cpA​<c means profit per unit is negative and the corner qsolar=0q_{\mathrm{solar}}=0qsolar​=0 applies. Stability of the interior solution follows from equation (29): profit per MW is decreasing in own capacity, so a small excess of capacity makes profit negative and deters further entry.

This arrow diagram describes the equilibrium as a fixed point and, at the same time, the algorithm used to compute it. Start from a candidate capacity vector kkk. Run the dispatch model of equations (22)-(26) for a representative set of hours to obtain prices and solar output, p(k)p(k)p(k) and q(k)q(k)q(k). Evaluate the profit of equation (31). If profit is positive in a zone, raise that zone's capacity; if negative, lower it. Repeat until profit is zero in every solar zone; the resulting vector is k∗k^*k∗.

Formally the equilibrium is a root of the system

Πz(k∗)=0for all solar zones z,\Pi_z(k^*)=0\quad\text{for all solar zones } z ,Πz​(k∗)=0for all solar zones z,

or equivalently a fixed point of an updating map such as kz↦kz⋅NPV Revenuez(k)/(czkz)k_z\mapsto k_z\cdot\text{NPV Revenue}_z(k)/(c_z k_z)kz​↦kz​⋅NPV Revenuez​(k)/(cz​kz​), which leaves kzk_zkz​ unchanged exactly when revenue per MW equals czc_zcz​.

The nested structure is the computational heart of the paper: every evaluation of profit requires solving the dispatch linear program for many hours. A unique solution is expected because revenue per MW is decreasing in capacity by the cannibalization effect of equation (29). In the stylized model the fixed point is available in closed form: profit per unit is the price minus ccc, the price is linear in solar output, and setting it equal to ccc yields equation (9) directly. The same loop, run under a different network, produces the counterfactual capacities of equation (37).

The investment cost is not taken from engineering data; it is recovered from the model by revealed preference, inverting the zero-profit condition.

Step 1. Start from equation (28), which is assumed to hold at the observed capacity vector kkk under the actual transmission network:

E[∑y∈Y∑hpzyh(k) qzyh(k)(1+r)y]=czkz.E\left[\sum_{y\in Y}\sum_h\frac{p_{zyh}(k)\,q_{zyh}(k)}{(1+r)^y}\right]=c_z k_z .E​y∈Y∑​h∑​(1+r)ypzyh​(k)qzyh​(k)​​=cz​kz​.
