cz=1kz E[∑y,hpzyh(k) qzyh(k)(1+r)y],c_z=\frac{1}{k_z}\,E\left[\sum_{y,h}\frac{p_{zyh}(k)\,q_{zyh}(k)}{(1+r)^y}\right],cz​=kz​1​E​y,h∑​(1+r)ypzyh​(k)qzyh​(k)​​,

which is the target. Everything on the right is known once the dispatch model has been solved at the observed kkk, so there is exactly one unknown per zone and one equation per zone: czc_zcz​ is just identified, with no residual.

Step 3 (reading the magnitude). Using the per-MW notation qzyh=azyhkzq_{zyh}=a_{zyh}k_zqzyh​=azyh​kz​ from the derivation of equation (28), czc_zcz​ is the discounted revenue of one MW. If annual revenue per MW were a constant RzR_zRz​ and payments arrived at the end of each of 25 years, the right side would be RzR_zRz​ times an annuity factor:

cz=Rz∑y=1251(1+r)y=Rz 1−(1+r)−25r≈13.0 Rzat r=0.0583.c_z=R_z\sum_{y=1}^{25}\frac{1}{(1+r)^y}=R_z\,\frac{1-(1+r)^{-25}}{r}\approx 13.0\,R_z\quad\text{at } r=0.0583 .cz​=Rz​y=1∑25​(1+r)y1​=Rz​r1−(1+r)−25​≈13.0Rz​at r=0.0583.

The timing convention is my illustration; the note does not say whether yyy starts at zero or one. Under it, the estimates c1=1.84c_1=1.84c1​=1.84 and c2=1.67c_2=1.67c2​=1.67 million USD per MW correspond to roughly 142142142 and 129129129 thousand USD of revenue per MW per year.

The identifying assumption is that observed capacity is a free-entry equilibrium with correct expectations about the integrated network: investors expected exactly the prices the model generates. If entry were still in progress, or if investors relied on subsidies or contracts outside the spot market, the recovered czc_zcz​ would absorb those factors. The closeness of the estimates to reported installation costs is the paper's check on this assumption.

The displayed symbol is the policy lever of the counterfactuals: the capacity flzf_{lz}flz​ of transmission line lll at zone zzz, in MW, the same parameter that bounds imports and exports in equations (24) and (25). The note singles it out because, once the investment costs have been recovered from equation (33), it is the only primitive that is changed across scenarios. Demand, fuel costs, thermal and hydro capacities, the discount rate and czc_zcz​ are all held at their estimated or observed values.

In practice two elements of the vector fff are manipulated: the capacity of the 2017 Antofagasta-Atacama interconnection and the capacity added by the 2019 Atacama-Santiago reinforcement. Writing the actual network as f1f^{1}f1 and the network without the two expansions as f0f^{0}f0,

flz0={flzpre-expansionif l is one of the two expanded lines,flz1otherwise.f^{0}_{lz}=\begin{cases} f^{\text{pre-expansion}}_{lz} & \text{if } l \text{ is one of the two expanded lines},\\ f^{1}_{lz} & \text{otherwise}.\end{cases}flz0​={flzpre-expansion​flz1​​if l is one of the two expanded lines,otherwise.​

For the interconnection the pre-expansion value is zero, since the northern and central systems were not connected at all; for the reinforcement it is the capacity of the older, weaker corridor.

Treating fff as exogenous is a maintained assumption: transmission is planned and regulated by the government, not built by solar investors, and the counterfactual asks what private investment would have done had the government not built the lines. The scenarios in equations (38)-(40) are defined by which of f0f^{0}f0 and f1f^{1}f1 is used and whether kkk is re-solved.

These are the two outputs of the dispatch model that enter the investor's problem, written as functions of the candidate capacity vector kkk: the zonal price pzyh(k)p_{zyh}(k)pzyh​(k) in zone zzz, year yyy and hour hhh (USD/MWh) and the solar generation qzyh(k)q_{zyh}(k)qzyh​(k) in the same zone and hour (MWh). They are the objects in equation (27) re-indexed by year and hour, because the investment condition discounts over the 25-year life of a plant.

The point of displaying them here is that in a counterfactual they must be recomputed, not taken from data. Observed prices were generated by the actual network and the actual capacity; under a different network, or a different kkk, the dispatch linear program of equations (22)-(26) returns different prices and possibly different solar output, since output per MW can fall when surplus is curtailed. For each candidate kkk the product

pzyh(k) qzyh(k)p_{zyh}(k)\,q_{zyh}(k)pzyh​(k)qzyh​(k)

is the spot revenue of zone-zzz solar in that hour, the integrand of equation (28).

The dependence on kkk is what makes the problem an equilibrium problem and not a simple calculation. A higher kzk_zkz​ raises qzyhq_{zyh}qzyh​ roughly proportionally but lowers pzyhp_{zyh}pzyh​ (equation (29)), so revenue per MW declines. The dependence is on the whole vector, so capacity in one zone affects revenue in another. The expectation in equation (28) is taken over the future paths of demand and fuel costs that determine these functions in later years.

The displayed symbol kz∗k_z^*kz∗​ is the unknown of the counterfactual exercise: the solar capacity in zone zzz (MW) at which, under the network being considered, investors just break even. It is defined implicitly by two requirements holding at once. Prices and quantities must be those of the cost-minimizing dispatch given k∗k^*k∗ (equations (22)-(27)), and at those prices the zero-profit condition must hold in every solar zone (equations (28) and (31)):

E[∑y∈Y∑hpzyh(k∗) qzyh(k∗)(1+r)y]=c^z kz∗∀z.E\left[\sum_{y\in Y}\sum_h\frac{p_{zyh}(k^*)\,q_{zyh}(k^*)}{(1+r)^y}\right]=\widehat c_z\,k_z^*\qquad\forall z .E​y∈Y∑​h∑​(1+r)ypzyh​(k∗)qzyh​(k∗)​​=cz​kz∗​∀z.

Compared with the estimation step, the roles of known and unknown are swapped. In equation (33) capacity is observed and the cost czc_zcz​ is solved for; here the cost is fixed at its estimate c^z\widehat c_zcz​ and capacity is solved for. Under the actual network the two steps are inverse to each other, so the model reproduces observed capacity exactly by construction; the content lies in what kz∗k_z^*kz∗​ becomes under another network.

Numerically the authors search over capacity (the loop of equation (32)) until the condition holds. The stylized analogue is equation (9), where the same two requirements, marginal-cost dispatch and the entry price ccc, give the equilibrium solar quantity in closed form under integration and zero under autarky. The empirical values for the no-integration network are reported in equations (42) and (43).

This schematic adds the network fff as an explicit argument to the fixed-point logic of equation (32), making clear how a change in transmission propagates. For a given network, dispatch delivers prices and solar output for every candidate capacity, p(k;f)p(k;f)p(k;f) and q(k;f)q(k;f)q(k;f). These determine profit,

Πz(k;f)=E[∑y∈Y∑hpzyh(k;f) qzyh(k;f)(1+r)y]−c^z kz,\Pi_z(k;f)=E\left[\sum_{y\in Y}\sum_h\frac{p_{zyh}(k;f)\,q_{zyh}(k;f)}{(1+r)^y}\right]-\widehat c_z\,k_z ,Πz​(k;f)=E​y∈Y∑​h∑​(1+r)ypzyh​(k;f)qzyh​(k;f)​​−cz​kz​,

and equilibrium capacity k∗(f)k^*(f)k∗(f) is the root of Π(k;f)=0\Pi(k;f)=0Π(k;f)=0.

The comparative static of interest is how the root moves with fff. By the implicit function theorem, for a single zone,

dk∗df=−∂Π/∂f∂Π/∂k>0,\frac{dk^*}{df}=-\frac{\partial\Pi/\partial f}{\partial\Pi/\partial k}>0 ,dfdk∗​=−∂Π/∂k∂Π/∂f​>0,

because more export capacity raises solar-hour prices in the solar zone, so the numerator is positive, while more capacity lowers profit per MW by equation (29), so the denominator is negative. The stylized model gives the two endpoints: k∗=0k^*=0k∗=0 with no line and the quantity in equation (9) with an unconstrained line.

The diagram also shows the two ways a network change affects outcomes such as cost. Holding kkk fixed, fff changes dispatch only: the short-run channel of equation (6). Letting kkk move to k∗(f)k^*(f)k∗(f) adds the long-run channel of equations (10)-(11). Scenarios 2 and 3 in equations (39) and (40) correspond to these two ways of evaluating the same change in fff.

Scenario 1 is the factual benchmark: the transmission network including both the 2017 interconnection and the 2019 reinforcement, combined with the solar capacity actually observed. In the notation of equation (37) it is the pair

(f1, kActual),kActual=k∗(f1),\big(f^{1},\ k^{\text{Actual}}\big),\qquad k^{\text{Actual}}=k^*(f^{1}),(f1, kActual),kActual=k∗(f1),

where f1f^{1}f1 denotes the actual network. The equality on the right is not a coincidence but a consequence of how the costs are estimated: equation (33) chooses czc_zcz​ so that observed capacity satisfies the zero-profit condition under the actual network. “Observed investment” and “equilibrium investment under integration” are thus the same thing in the model.

Even though this scenario corresponds to reality, its outcomes (costs, prices, solar generation) are computed by simulating the dispatch model, not read from the raw data. Using simulated outcomes for all three scenarios ensures that differences between scenarios reflect only the changes in fff and kkk, and not model error that would appear on one side of the comparison only.

Scenario 1 is the common minuend of both comparisons in the paper: subtracting Scenario 2 (equation (39)) gives the gains from trade with fixed capacity, and subtracting Scenario 3 (equation (40)) gives the full effect boxed in equation (41). In the stylized model it is the long-run integrated equilibrium with price ccc and solar quantity from equation (9).

Scenario 2 removes the two transmission expansions but keeps solar capacity at its observed level:

(f0, kActual),\big(f^{0},\ k^{\text{Actual}}\big),(f0, kActual),

with f0f^{0}f0 the network without the 2017 and 2019 lines. Only the dispatch model is re-run; the investment condition is deliberately not imposed, so in this scenario solar plants are generally making losses.

This is the counterfactual implicitly used by a conventional analysis that takes plants as given, and it is also what the event study approximates: the world just before the lines opened, when the anticipatory solar was already in place. In the stylized model it is the transition state of equations (12)-(15), with regions separated, solar installed, and a depressed price p~A\widetilde p_Ap​A​ in the solar region.

The difference between Scenarios 1 and 2 isolates the reallocation channel of equation (6): the same plants, dispatched with and without the lines. It is not the policy effect, because Scenario 2 is not an equilibrium: the capacity kActualk^{\text{Actual}}kActual would never have been built facing the network f0f^{0}f0. Two distortions follow, both visible in the results. The cost and solar-generation effects are understated, since the solar plants are credited to the no-integration world (equations (44)-(49)). The price gap is overstated, since stranded solar pushes the northern price toward zero (equation (50)).

Scenario 3 removes the two transmission expansions and lets solar capacity re-equilibrate:

(f0, k∗(f0)),\big(f^{0},\ k^*(f^{0})\big),(f0, k∗(f0)),

where k∗(f0)k^*(f^{0})k∗(f0) solves the zero-profit condition of equation (28) under the no-expansion network, at the investment costs recovered in equation (33). Both blocks of the model are used: dispatch for prices, free entry for capacity.

This is the paper's answer to the question of what Chile would look like had market integration never happened and never been expected. It is the state that equation (16) says is missing from the data. In the stylized model it is the plain autarky equilibrium of equation (3): no solar, since pA<cp_A<cpA​<c, and a price in region AAA of pAp_ApA​, not the depressed p~A\widetilde p_Ap​A​.

Relative to Scenario 2, solar capacity is much lower: about 20 percent and 17 percent of actual capacity in the two northern zones (equations (42)-(43)). Thermal plants therefore run more and costs are higher, while the northern price is no longer crushed by stranded solar. The difference between Scenarios 2 and 3 is thus the investment effect of equation (1).

The credibility of Scenario 3 rests on the maintained assumptions of the investment block: free entry with constant cost per MW, revenue from the spot market at zonal prices, and no change in other generation investment. The last means only solar capacity is re-solved, while thermal, hydro and wind capacities are held fixed.

The boxed difference is the paper's definition of the total long-run effect of market integration: any outcome YYY (generation cost, solar output, emissions, the price gap) evaluated in Scenario 1 minus the same outcome in Scenario 3,

Y(f1,k∗(f1))−Y(f0,k∗(f0)).Y\big(f^{1},k^*(f^{1})\big)-Y\big(f^{0},k^*(f^{0})\big).Y(f1,k∗(f1))−Y(f0,k∗(f0)).

Both terms are long-run equilibria in which capacity is consistent with the network, so the comparison is between two internally coherent worlds.

Adding and subtracting the Scenario 2 outcome splits this total into the two channels of equation (1):

Y(f1,k∗(f1))−Y(f0,k∗(f1))⏟gains from trade (Scenario 1−Scenario 2)+Y(f0,k∗(f1))−Y(f0,k∗(f0))⏟investment effect (Scenario 2−Scenario 3).\underbrace{Y\big(f^{1},k^*(f^{1})\big)-Y\big(f^{0},k^*(f^{1})\big)}_{\text{gains from trade (Scenario 1}-\text{Scenario 2)}} +\underbrace{Y\big(f^{0},k^*(f^{1})\big)-Y\big(f^{0},k^*(f^{0})\big)}_{\text{investment effect (Scenario 2}-\text{Scenario 3)}} .gains from trade (Scenario 1−Scenario 2)Y(f1,k∗(f1))−Y(f0,k∗(f1))​​+investment effect (Scenario 2−Scenario 3)Y(f0,k∗(f1))−Y(f0,k∗(f0))​​.

The decomposition is path-dependent in the usual way: one could instead change capacity first and the network second, and the split would differ, though the total would not. The paper's ordering is the natural one because Scenario 2 corresponds to what a fixed-capacity analysis delivers.

The two terms need not have the same sign. For generation cost and solar output both are favorable and the total exceeds the fixed-capacity effect (equations (44)-(49)). For the price gap the second term is negative: stranded solar in Scenario 2 inflates the gap, so the total convergence effect of 8 USD/MWh is far smaller than the fixed-capacity figure of 47.6 USD/MWh (equations (52) and (54)).

This is the first quantitative output of the investment model: for zone 1, Antofagasta, the free-entry capacity under the network without the two expansions is about one fifth of the capacity actually observed. In the notation of equation (37), the left side is k1∗(f0)k_1^*(f^{0})k1∗​(f0) and the right side involves k1∗(f1)k_1^*(f^{1})k1∗​(f1). Equivalently,

k1Actual−k1NoIntegrationk1Actual≈0.80,\frac{k_1^{Actual}-k_1^{NoIntegration}}{k_1^{Actual}}\approx 0.80 ,k1Actual​k1Actual​−k1NoIntegration​​≈0.80,

so roughly 80 percent of the solar capacity in Antofagasta is attributable to market integration.

The number comes from solving the zero-profit condition of equation (28) at the estimated cost c1=1.84c_1=1.84c1​=1.84 million USD per MW with f=f0f=f^{0}f=f0. Without the interconnection, Antofagasta's northern system is an island whose demand is limited relative to its solar potential. Additional solar quickly saturates midday demand and drives midday prices toward zero, so revenue per MW falls below c1c_1c1​ at a small capacity: the cannibalization curve of equation (29) is steep. With the lines, the same curve is much flatter because midday output can be exported south.

The stylized model predicts an even starker result, zero solar without integration, since there pA<cp_A<cpA​<c is assumed. The empirical answer is not zero because there is some local demand at prices that cover costs for the first units of solar. The estimate is a model prediction conditional on the recovered cost and on holding other capacity fixed; it is not directly observable.

This is the corresponding result for zone 2, Atacama: without the transmission expansions, equilibrium solar capacity would be about 17 percent of what was actually built, so about 83 percent of Atacama's solar capacity is attributed to integration:

k2Actual−k2NoIntegrationk2Actual≈0.83.\frac{k_2^{Actual}-k_2^{NoIntegration}}{k_2^{Actual}}\approx 0.83 .k2Actual​k2Actual​−k2NoIntegration​​≈0.83.

It is computed in the same way as equation (42), solving the zero-profit condition (28) under the no-expansion network at the estimated cost c2=1.67c_2=1.67c2​=1.67 million USD per MW. The two zones are solved jointly, because they are connected and their solar output competes for the same export corridor.

Atacama's dependence on transmission is, if anything, stronger than Antofagasta's. It has excellent solar resources and little local demand, and it sits on the weak pre-2019 corridor toward Santiago; before the reinforcement its midday prices were frequently near zero, the empirical counterpart of the depressed transition price p~A\widetilde p_Ap​A​ in equation (15). The reinforcement is what lets its output reach the main demand center.

Together, equations (42) and (43) are the basis for the headline results that follow. Because Scenario 3 has only about a fifth of the solar capacity of Scenario 2, the two scenarios differ sharply in solar generation (equations (44)-(45)), in generation cost (equations (46)-(49)), and in northern prices and hence the price gap (equations (50)-(54)).

This number is the effect of market integration on solar generation when solar capacity is held fixed, that is the comparison of Scenario 1 with Scenario 2 (equations (38)-(39)). With GsG_sGs​ denoting total solar generation in Scenario sss, it reads

G1−G2G2≈10%.\frac{G_1-G_2}{G_2}\approx 10\% .G2​G1​−G2​​≈10%.

Since the installed panels are identical in the two scenarios, the potential output is the same; the only reason generation can differ is curtailment. Without the lines, the observed capacity in the north produces more at midday than local demand plus the old export limits can absorb (the ceiling discussed under equation (25)), and the surplus is spilled. Building the lines removes most of that spill. The 10 percent is therefore a pure dispatch effect, the solar-specific face of the gains-from-trade channel of equation (6).

The number is small because curtailment, even when severe in some hours, affects a limited share of annual output. It is the figure a fixed-capacity analysis would report as “the effect of transmission on renewable generation”, and it serves as the benchmark against which the full effect in equation (45) is judged. The values are as reported in the note; I read the percentage as relative to the no-integration scenario.

This boxed number is the full effect of market integration on solar generation, comparing Scenario 1 with Scenario 3 (equations (38) and (40)), in which solar capacity is re-solved under the no-expansion network. In the notation used for equation (44),

G1−G3G3≈178%⟺G1≈2.78 G3,\frac{G_1-G_3}{G_3}\approx 178\%\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G_1\approx 2.78\,G_3 ,G3​G1​−G3​​≈178%⟺G1​≈2.78G3​,

so actual solar generation is nearly three times what it would be in a world without the lines.

The contrast with the 10 percent of equation (44) is the paper's headline for renewables: more than nine tenths of the increase in solar generation comes from plants that would not exist without integration, not from better use of existing plants. The source is the capacity result of equations (42)-(43): in Scenario 3 the two northern zones have only about 20 and 17 percent of their actual capacity.

A consistency check on magnitudes: if all solar were in those two zones and output were proportional to capacity, a fall in capacity to roughly a fifth would imply G1≈5 G3G_1\approx 5\,G_3G1​≈5G3​, an increase of about 400 percent. The reported 178 percent is smaller, which is what one expects given that solar located in other zones is unchanged across scenarios and that the smaller counterfactual fleet suffers less curtailment per MW. This is my reading of the magnitudes, not a calculation reported in the note.

This is the change in average generation cost attributed to market integration when solar capacity is held fixed: Scenario 1 relative to Scenario 2. With c(s)c^{(s)}c(s) the system-wide average generation cost per MWh in Scenario sss,

c(1)−c(2)c(2)≈−3%.\frac{c^{(1)}-c^{(2)}}{c^{(2)}}\approx -3\% .c(2)c(1)−c(2)​≈−3%.

It measures the static reallocation channel of equation (6): with the same plants, the lines allow cheap northern generation, including solar that would otherwise be curtailed, to displace more expensive thermal generation near Santiago. It is the structural-model counterpart of the reduced-form coefficients β1+β2\beta_1+\beta_2β1​+β2​ in equation (18), which also condition on installed capacity through the merit-order cost ct∗c_t^*ct∗​. That the regression and Scenario 1 minus Scenario 2 give similar magnitudes is one of the paper's validations of the dispatch model.

In the stylized model this effect corresponds to the event-study quantity ΔES\Delta^{\text{ES}}ΔES of equation (17), the cost difference between the transition state and the integrated state with the same solar. A 3 percent saving is economically meaningful for a national power system, but the next equation shows that it is well under half of the full effect.

This boxed number is the full effect of market integration on average generation cost: Scenario 1 relative to Scenario 3, with solar capacity re-equilibrated in the no-integration world,

c(1)−c(3)c(3)≈−8%.\frac{c^{(1)}-c^{(3)}}{c^{(3)}}\approx -8\% .c(3)c(1)−c(3)​≈−8%.

Comparing with equation (46), accounting for investment raises the estimated cost saving from 3 to 8 percent, a factor of about 2.7. The extra saving comes from the zero-marginal-cost solar output that exists only because of the lines and that displaces fuel-burning plants in every hour in which it produces. In terms of the decomposition in equation (41), roughly 3 points are gains from trade and roughly 5 points are the investment effect, up to the usual base differences in percentages.

This is the empirical counterpart of equation (17): the fixed-capacity (event-study) effect understates the full effect. Two caveats on interpretation. First, the figure refers to generation (operating) cost. Solar entry is not free; by the zero-profit condition (28) its investment cost equals its market revenue, so a welfare statement requires netting investment costs out, which the paper does in its cost-benefit analysis of the lines. Second, lower thermal generation also lowers emissions, an additional benefit outside this number.

This is the fixed-capacity effect of equation (46) recomputed for the noon hour only: the generation cost per MWh at midday is about 7 percent lower in Scenario 1 than in Scenario 2.

The effect is more than twice the all-hours figure of 3 percent because noon is when the constraint relaxed by the lines actually binds. Solar output peaks at midday, so that is when the north has the largest surplus of zero-cost power, when the old export limits of equation (25) were most often congested, and when curtailment in the no-line scenario is greatest. Writing the all-hours effect as a weighted average of hourly effects,

Δcall=∑hwh Δch,∑hwh=1,\Delta c^{\text{all}}=\sum_h w_h\,\Delta c_h ,\qquad \sum_h w_h=1 ,Δcall=h∑​wh​Δch​,h∑​wh​=1,

with weights whw_hwh​ given by hourly shares of generation, the noon component is large while night-time components are close to zero, since at night there is no solar to move and the lines matter only for thermal reallocation.

The same hour-of-day pattern appears in the reduced form: the note reports larger coefficients at noon (−2.42-2.42−2.42 and −0.96-0.96−0.96 USD/MWh) than for all hours (−2.07-2.07−2.07 and −0.62-0.62−0.62) in equation (18). The noon comparison is therefore a sharper test of the mechanism, and the next equation shows how it changes when investment adjusts.

This boxed number is the full effect at noon: generation cost per MWh at midday is about 18 percent lower in Scenario 1 than in Scenario 3, where solar capacity is re-solved without the lines.

It is the largest of the four cost numbers, and the ordering of the four is itself informative:

−3%⏟all hours, fixed k ,−7%⏟noon, fixed k ,−8%⏟all hours, endogenous k ,−18%⏟noon, endogenous k .\underbrace{-3\%}_{\text{all hours, fixed } k}\ ,\qquad \underbrace{-7\%}_{\text{noon, fixed } k}\ ,\qquad \underbrace{-8\%}_{\text{all hours, endogenous } k}\ ,\qquad \underbrace{-18\%}_{\text{noon, endogenous } k}\ .all hours, fixed k−3%​​ ,noon, fixed k−7%​​ ,all hours, endogenous k−8%​​ ,noon, endogenous k−18%​​ .

Moving from all hours to noon multiplies the effect by a bit more than two under either treatment of capacity; moving from fixed to endogenous capacity multiplies it by about 2.6 in either hour window. The investment channel is thus concentrated in exactly the hours when solar produces, as it should be if the extra saving comes from solar plants that integration caused to be built: at noon those plants displace thermal generation one for one, while at night they contribute nothing.

The 11-point gap between equations (48) and (49) is the noon-hour investment effect. It is the clearest quantitative expression of the claim in equation (17) that a fixed-capacity or before-after comparison captures well under half of the long-run cost reduction.

This number is the average price gap between Santiago and Atacama in Scenario 2: no transmission expansion, but solar capacity kept at its observed level (equation (39)). Formally it is the difference in average zonal prices from the dispatch model of equation (27),

Gap2=pˉSantiago(f0,kActual)−pˉAtacama(f0,kActual)≈54 USD/MWh.\text{Gap}_2=\bar p_{\text{Santiago}}\big(f^{0},k^{\text{Actual}}\big)-\bar p_{\text{Atacama}}\big(f^{0},k^{\text{Actual}}\big)\approx 54\ \text{USD/MWh}.Gap2​=pˉ​Santiago​(f0,kActual)−pˉ​Atacama​(f0,kActual)≈54 USD/MWh.

The gap is very large because this scenario strands the observed solar fleet behind a weak corridor. In solar hours Atacama has far more zero-cost output than it can use or export, the export bound of equation (25) binds, solar is curtailed and the local price collapses toward zero; Santiago, cut off from that power, is served by expensive thermal units. By the congestion condition under equation (23), the price difference then equals the shadow value of the line, which is at its maximum.

In the stylized model this is the transition gap pB−p~Ap_B-\widetilde p_ApB​−p​A​ of equation (15), which exceeds the true autarky gap pB−pAp_B-p_ApB​−pA​ by βAqsolar\beta_A q_{\mathrm{solar}}βA​qsolar​. The 54 USD/MWh is therefore not a measure of how far apart prices would have been without integration; it is how far apart they are when investors have already built for an integrated market that has not yet arrived. It is the starting point of the fixed-capacity convergence calculation in equation (52).

This is the Santiago-Atacama average price gap in Scenario 1, the actual integrated market with observed solar capacity (equation (38)):

Gap1=pˉSantiago(f1,kActual)−pˉAtacama(f1,kActual)≈6.4 USD/MWh.\text{Gap}_1=\bar p_{\text{Santiago}}\big(f^{1},k^{\text{Actual}}\big)-\bar p_{\text{Atacama}}\big(f^{1},k^{\text{Actual}}\big)\approx 6.4\ \text{USD/MWh}.Gap1​=pˉ​Santiago​(f1,kActual)−pˉ​Atacama​(f1,kActual)≈6.4 USD/MWh.

It is small but not zero, in contrast to the stylized model, where full integration gives a single price p∗p^*p∗ (equation (5)) or ccc (equation (7)). Two features of the dispatch model keep a positive gap even with the new lines. First, transmission losses: by the condition under equation (23), even on an uncongested line the importing zone's price exceeds the exporter's by the loss wedge, since only the fraction 1−δ11-\delta_11−δ1​ of the power sent arrives. Second, the expanded lines have finite capacity (equations (24)-(25)) and still congest in some hours, mostly around midday with high solar output, and in those hours prices separate.

This number is the common endpoint of both convergence calculations. Subtracting it from the Scenario 2 gap gives the fixed-capacity convergence of equation (52); subtracting it from the Scenario 3 gap of equation (53) gives the long-run convergence of equation (54). Since the endpoint is shared, the whole difference between the two calculations comes from which no-integration world is used as the starting point.

Define price convergence due to integration as the reduction in the Santiago-Atacama price gap from the no-integration world to the integrated world. If the no-integration world is taken to be Scenario 2, in which solar capacity is held at its observed level, the calculation uses the gaps of equations (50) and (51).

Step 1. Write the definition with fixed capacity:

Convergencefixed k=Gap2−Gap1.\text{Convergence}^{\text{fixed } k}=\text{Gap}_2-\text{Gap}_1 .Convergencefixed k=Gap2​−Gap1​.

Step 2. Insert the two numbers:

54−6.4=47.6 USD/MWh.54-6.4=47.6\ \text{USD/MWh}.54−6.4=47.6 USD/MWh.

Read at face value, this says integration removed about 88 percent of the price gap, since 47.6/54≈0.8847.6/54\approx 0.8847.6/54≈0.88. It is the figure an analysis that ignores investment responses would report, and it is close in spirit to what a before-after comparison of observed price gaps would find, because the observed pre-period also had anticipatory solar in place.

Step 3 (why it is misleading). In the stylized model the same calculation gives

(pB−p~A)−0=(pB−pA)+βA qsolar,(p_B-\widetilde p_A)-0=(p_B-p_A)+\beta_A\,q_{\mathrm{solar}} ,(pB​−p​A​)−0=(pB​−pA​)+βA​qsolar​,

using equation (15): the measured convergence equals the true autarky gap plus a term due solely to solar that was built because of the line. That extra term is an artifact of the wrong counterfactual, and equation (54) removes it.

This is the Santiago-Atacama price gap in Scenario 3: no transmission expansion and solar capacity re-solved under free entry (equation (40)):

Gap3=pˉSantiago(f0,k∗(f0))−pˉAtacama(f0,k∗(f0))≈14.4 USD/MWh.\text{Gap}_3=\bar p_{\text{Santiago}}\big(f^{0},k^*(f^{0})\big)-\bar p_{\text{Atacama}}\big(f^{0},k^*(f^{0})\big)\approx 14.4\ \text{USD/MWh}.Gap3​=pˉ​Santiago​(f0,k∗(f0))−pˉ​Atacama​(f0,k∗(f0))≈14.4 USD/MWh.

It is far below the 54 USD/MWh of Scenario 2 (equation (50)) even though the network is the same in both. The whole difference comes from solar capacity. In Scenario 3 investors build only about a fifth of the actual capacity in the north (equations (42)-(43)), precisely the amount at which northern solar-hour prices are high enough to cover the investment cost. The zero-profit condition (28) thus rules out a collapsed northern price as a long-run outcome: prices near zero in solar hours and positive solar investment cannot coexist in equilibrium.

In the stylized model this is the true autarky gap pB−pAp_B-p_ApB​−pA​ from equation (3), as opposed to the transition gap pB−p~Ap_B-\widetilde p_ApB​−p​A​. The remaining 14.4 USD/MWh reflects genuine differences in the cost of serving the two regions when they are poorly connected.

The ranking of the three gaps, 54 above 14.4 above 6.4, summarizes the argument: integration does narrow the gap, but most of the apparent narrowing in a fixed-capacity comparison is the unwinding of a gap that anticipatory investment itself created.

Repeat the convergence calculation of equation (52) with the correct long-run counterfactual: the no-integration world is Scenario 3, in which solar capacity has adjusted to the absence of the lines.

Step 1. Definition with endogenous capacity, using the gaps of equations (53) and (51):

Convergenceendogenous k=Gap3−Gap1.\text{Convergence}^{\text{endogenous } k}=\text{Gap}_3-\text{Gap}_1 .Convergenceendogenous k=Gap3​−Gap1​.

Step 2. Insert the numbers:

14.4−6.4=8 USD/MWh,14.4-6.4=8\ \text{USD/MWh},14.4−6.4=8 USD/MWh,

which is the boxed result.

Step 3 (size of the bias). Subtracting this from equation (52), the endpoint Gap1\text{Gap}_1Gap1​ cancels:

47.6−8=Gap2−Gap3=54−14.4=39.6 USD/MWh.47.6-8=\text{Gap}_2-\text{Gap}_3=54-14.4=39.6\ \text{USD/MWh}.47.6−8=Gap2​−Gap3​=54−14.4=39.6 USD/MWh.

So about 83 percent of the fixed-capacity convergence figure (39.6/47.6≈0.8339.6/47.6\approx 0.8339.6/47.6≈0.83) is not an effect of integration relative to a world without it; it is the price depression caused by solar that was built only because integration was coming. The fixed-capacity figure overstates true convergence by a factor of about six (47.6/8≈647.6/8\approx 647.6/8≈6).

Step 4 (sign of the bias versus equation (17)). In the stylized model the overstatement is βAqsolar>0\beta_A q_{\mathrm{solar}}>0βA​qsolar​>0 (see the derivation of equation (52)). The direction is opposite to the cost result: ignoring investment understates the cost and solar-generation effects (equations (44)-(49)) but overstates price convergence. Both biases have the same origin, namely treating an anticipation-contaminated state as the no-policy counterfactual, as in equation (16).

This is the first line of a three-line flow chart (equations (55)-(57)) summarizing how the one structural parameter per zone, the solar investment cost, is identified. The line lists the data inputs: the solar capacity actually installed in each zone, kzk_zkz​, and the actual transmission network fff, including the 2017 and 2019 lines.

The “plus” is a pairing, not arithmetic. Its content is an assumption: the observed pair is treated as a point on the long-run equilibrium locus,

kActual=k∗(fActual),k^{\text{Actual}}=k^*\big(f^{\text{Actual}}\big),kActual=k∗(fActual),

so that observed capacity is the free-entry response to the observed network in the sense of equation (37). Three things are assumed in that statement. Entry is competitive, so profits are zero and not merely non-negative. Investors correctly anticipated the integrated network when they built, which is consistent with the anticipation story of equations (12)-(15). And the capacity observed at the end of the sample is the equilibrium level and not a stock still adjusting.

Nothing else about solar investment is observed or needed: no bids, no project-level costs, no financing terms. This parsimony is possible because the Chilean cost-based dispatch makes the revenue side computable from engineering and cost data, as the next line of the chart shows.

This is the second line of the identification chart. The observed capacity and network of equation (55) are fed into the dispatch model of equations (22)-(26), which returns the hourly zonal prices and solar generation that prevail at that capacity, p(k)p(k)p(k) and q(k)q(k)q(k).

Model-generated prices are used, not just observed historical prices, because the zero-profit condition (28) requires expected revenue over the whole 25-year life of a plant,

E[∑y∈Y∑hpzyh(k) qzyh(k)(1+r)y],E\left[\sum_{y\in Y}\sum_h\frac{p_{zyh}(k)\,q_{zyh}(k)}{(1+r)^y}\right],E​y∈Y∑​h∑​(1+r)ypzyh​(k)qzyh​(k)​​,

and most of that horizon lies in the future. The dispatch model supplies prices for years not yet observed, given projections of demand and costs. Using it also guarantees internal consistency, since the same mapping from capacity to prices is used in estimation and in the counterfactuals of equation (37).

This step involves no estimation in the statistical sense. The dispatch model is calibrated from plant-level cost and capacity data, demand, and network parameters, and its fit is checked against observed generation costs and prices. Its accuracy is what the identification of the investment cost ultimately rests on. If the model overpredicted northern solar-hour prices, the implied cost in equation (57) would be too high, and the counterfactual capacity would be biased accordingly.

This third line closes the estimation chart: the simulated prices and quantities of equation (56) are inserted into the zero-profit condition, which is then solved for the investment cost per MW in each solar zone. The explicit formula is equation (33):

c^z=1kz E[∑y,hpzyh(k) qzyh(k)(1+r)y].\widehat c_z=\frac{1}{k_z}\,E\left[\sum_{y,h}\frac{p_{zyh}(k)\,q_{zyh}(k)}{(1+r)^y}\right].cz​=kz​1​E​y,h∑​(1+r)ypzyh​(k)qzyh​(k)​​.

The estimator is a method-of-moments estimator in its simplest form: one moment condition (zero profit) and one unknown per zone, so the model is exactly identified and c^z\widehat c_zcz​ makes the condition hold with no residual. There is no sampling error in the usual sense; the uncertainty lies in the model inputs and assumptions, namely the discount rate r=0.0583r=0.0583r=0.0583, the 25-year lifetime and the projected price paths. The hat distinguishes the recovered value from the true cost czc_zcz​.

Because there are no overidentifying restrictions, validation must come from outside the model. The note reports about 1.84 and 1.67 million USD per MW for the two northern zones, close to installation costs reported for utility-scale solar in Chile in that period. This supports the free-entry interpretation and gives some confidence that the same c^z\widehat c_zcz​ can be carried to counterfactual networks in equation (58).

This line opens the second chart (equations (58)-(60)), which describes the counterfactual simulation. Its inputs are the estimated investment costs from equation (57) and a transmission network different from the actual one, for instance the network without the 2017 interconnection and the 2019 reinforcement.

Pairing an estimated parameter with a changed policy variable is the essence of a structural counterfactual, and it rests on an invariance assumption:

cz(fCF)=cz(fActual)=c^z.c_z\big(f^{\text{CF}}\big)=c_z\big(f^{\text{Actual}}\big)=\widehat c_z .cz​(fCF)=cz​(fActual)=cz​.

The cost of building a MW of solar in a zone is a technological and financial primitive that does not depend on whether the transmission lines exist. This is plausible: panel prices are set in world markets, and land and labor costs in the Atacama desert are unlikely to change with the grid. It would fail if, say, the lines lowered construction or connection costs directly, or if financing terms depended on integration.

Everything else in the environment (demand, thermal and hydro fleets, fuel prices, the discount rate) is also held at the values used in estimation. Only two things are allowed to differ from the factual world: the network, by assumption, and solar capacity, by equilibrium. Counterfactual capacity is therefore not an input on this line; it is an output, obtained in equations (59) and (60).

This second line of the counterfactual chart states the two conditions imposed jointly under the counterfactual network. The dispatch equilibrium requires that, given capacities and the network, generation and flows solve the cost-minimization problem of equations (22)-(26), with prices equal to its shadow values (equation (27)). The investment equilibrium requires that, at those prices, solar profit is zero in each solar zone (equations (28) and (31)). Together they define the system

Πz(k;fCF)=E[∑y∈Y∑hpzyh(k;fCF) qzyh(k;fCF)(1+r)y]−c^z kz=0∀z,\Pi_z\big(k;f^{\text{CF}}\big)=E\left[\sum_{y\in Y}\sum_h\frac{p_{zyh}(k;f^{\text{CF}})\,q_{zyh}(k;f^{\text{CF}})}{(1+r)^y}\right]-\widehat c_z\,k_z=0\qquad\forall z ,Πz​(k;fCF)=E​y∈Y∑​h∑​(1+r)ypzyh​(k;fCF)qzyh​(k;fCF)​​−cz​kz​=0∀z,

to be solved for kkk.

The “plus” again means simultaneity. The two conditions are nested: dispatch is an inner optimization solved for each trial kkk, and the zero-profit condition is the outer equation, as in the loop of equation (32). Imposing only the first condition, with capacity left at its observed level, yields Scenario 2 (equation (39)); imposing both yields Scenario 3 (equation (40)).

The contrast with the estimation chart is instructive. In equations (55)-(57) the dispatch model is solved once, at observed capacity, and the zero-profit condition is solved for cost. Here the cost is known, the zero-profit condition is solved for capacity, and the dispatch model must be solved repeatedly along the search.

This final line lists the outputs of the counterfactual simulation. kzCFk_z^{CF}kzCF​ is the free-entry solar capacity of each zone under the counterfactual network, kzCF=kz∗(fCF)k_z^{CF}=k_z^*(f^{\text{CF}})kzCF​=kz∗​(fCF) in the notation of equation (37). pCFp^{CF}pCF and qCFq^{CF}qCF are the zonal prices and the generation by technology from the dispatch model evaluated at that capacity. CostCFCost^{CF}CostCF is the associated total (or per-MWh) generation cost, the minimized value of the objective in equation (22):

CostCF=∑z,t,jCztj(qztjCF).Cost^{CF}=\sum_{z,t,j}C_{ztj}\big(q^{CF}_{ztj}\big).CostCF=z,t,j∑​Cztj​(qztjCF​).

Each headline number in the note is a contrast between these outputs and their Scenario 1 counterparts. The capacity ratios of equations (42)-(43) compare kzCFk_z^{CF}kzCF​ with observed capacity. The solar-generation effects of equations (44)-(45) use the solar component of qCFq^{CF}qCF. The cost effects of equations (46)-(49) use CostCFCost^{CF}CostCF for all hours and for noon. The price gaps of equations (50)-(54) use pCFp^{CF}pCF in Santiago and Atacama.

Further outcomes follow mechanically from the same objects: emissions, by applying emission factors to thermal generation in qCFq^{CF}qCF, and consumer and producer surplus, from pCFp^{CF}pCF and costs. This is how the paper extends the analysis to pollution and to a cost-benefit evaluation of the transmission investment. Running the chart with capacity fixed at its observed level instead of solved gives the Scenario 2 versions of the same outputs.

This is the first of three lines (equations (61)-(63)) that restate the paper's mechanism as a causal chain, now for renewables in general and not only for solar in Chile. It covers the physical and market-access part of the chain.

“Transmission expansion” is an increase in the line capacities flzf_{lz}flz​. “Relaxed spatial constraints” refers to the bounds of equations (24)-(25): the set of feasible dispatches grows, so the minimized cost in equation (22) cannot rise. “Higher export opportunities” is the consequence for a resource-rich zone: in hours when it has surplus low-cost power, more of it can be sold elsewhere. In price terms, by the condition under equation (23),

(1−δ1) pz′t−pzt=μlt ≥0,(1-\delta_1)\,p_{z't}-p_{zt}=\mu_{lt}\ \geq 0 ,(1−δ1​)pz′t​−pzt​=μlt​ ≥0,

and expansion lowers the congestion multiplier μlt\mu_{lt}μlt​, pulling the exporting zone's price pztp_{zt}pzt​ up toward the importing zone's price.

The stylized counterpart is the move from autarky to integration in equations (3)-(5), where the price in region AAA rises from pAp_ApA​ to p∗p^*p∗ and region AAA becomes an exporter. Up to this point the chain is the standard trade argument. What distinguishes the paper is the next link, in equation (62), where this change in market access feeds into investment.

This second line of the chain is the investment link, the generalization of equation (11). Higher export opportunities raise the prices that a renewable plant in the resource-rich zone expects to earn in the hours when it produces, and therefore its expected discounted revenue per MW, the left side of the zero-profit condition (28) divided by kzk_zkz​:

1kz E[∑y∈Y∑hpzyh(k;f) qzyh(k;f)(1+r)y] rises with f.\frac{1}{k_z}\,E\left[\sum_{y\in Y}\sum_h\frac{p_{zyh}(k;f)\,q_{zyh}(k;f)}{(1+r)^y}\right]\ \text{rises with } f .kz​1​E​y∈Y∑​h∑​(1+r)ypzyh​(k;f)qzyh​(k;f)​​ rises with f.

With the investment cost czc_zcz​ unchanged, revenue per MW now exceeds cost at the old capacity, so entry occurs and continues until cannibalization (equation (29)) restores zero profit at a larger capacity k∗(f)k^*(f)k∗(f), as in equation (37).

The word expected is essential. Investment responds to anticipated revenue over the life of the plant, so it responds when the line becomes credible, not when it is energized. This timing is what breaks the before-after design (equations (12)-(16)).

Two features make renewables especially sensitive to this link. The resource is location-specific, so the best sites are often far from demand, as with the Atacama desert and Santiago. And output is concentrated in the same hours for all plants in a zone, so without export capacity local prices collapse quickly as capacity grows. Transmission is thus complementary to renewable investment. The empirical magnitude is given by equations (42)-(43): roughly four fifths of northern solar capacity depends on the lines.

This last line of the chain states the consequences of the induced entry for system outcomes. New renewable plants have near-zero marginal cost, so they enter at the bottom of the merit order and displace the most expensive units running in each hour, typically coal, gas or diesel plants. The variable cost of serving demand falls by the cost of the displaced generation:

Δ Costt≈− MCtdisplaced×Δqtrenewable,\Delta\,\text{Cost}_t\approx-\,MC^{\text{displaced}}_t\times\Delta q^{\text{renewable}}_t ,ΔCostt​≈−MCtdisplaced​×Δqtrenewable​,

and emissions fall by the emission rate of the displaced units times the same quantity.

This gain comes on top of the reallocation gain of equation (6), and it is the difference between the fixed-capacity and full cost effects reported in the note: 3 versus 8 percent for all hours, and 7 versus 18 percent at noon (equations (46)-(49)). In the stylized model it is the fall in nonsolar output from the quantities of equation (5) to those of equation (7).

Two qualifications apply. The cost reduction refers to operating costs; the new plants carry investment costs which, under free entry, exactly absorb their market revenue (equation (28)). The net social gain from the investment channel is therefore the fuel saving in excess of the solar investment cost, plus avoided external costs such as pollution, not the gross fuel saving. And because private investors do not capture those external benefits, the chain implies that the social return to transmission exceeds what a static dispatch analysis suggests.

This boxed inequality is the methodological message of the paper, a general version of equation (16). An observed before-after effect compares outcomes just after a policy takes effect with outcomes just before. The full long-run policy effect compares the world with the policy to the world in which the policy never existed and was never expected. The two coincide only if nothing that agents did before the implementation date was caused by the policy.

With forward-looking investment and an announced policy, that condition fails. Let Y(f,k)Y(f,k)Y(f,k) be an outcome as a function of the network and capacity, with f0,f1f^{0},f^{1}f0,f1 the networks before and after and k0,k1k^{0},k^{1}k0,k1 the corresponding equilibrium capacities. If capacity k1k^{1}k1 is already in place when the line opens,

Y(f1,k1)−Y(f0,k1)⏟before-after ≠ Y(f1,k1)−Y(f0,k0)⏟full effect,\underbrace{Y(f^{1},k^{1})-Y(f^{0},k^{1})}_{\text{before-after}}\ \neq\ \underbrace{Y(f^{1},k^{1})-Y(f^{0},k^{0})}_{\text{full effect}} ,before-afterY(f1,k1)−Y(f0,k1)​​ = full effectY(f1,k1)−Y(f0,k0)​​,

and the discrepancy, Y(f0,k0)−Y(f0,k1)Y(f^{0},k^{0})-Y(f^{0},k^{1})Y(f0,k0)−Y(f0,k1), is the effect of anticipatory investment on the pre-period.

The sign of the discrepancy depends on the outcome. For generation cost and renewable output the before-after effect is too small (equation (17) and equations (44)-(49)); for price convergence it is too large (equations (52) and (54)). The bias is therefore not a simple attenuation that could be corrected by scaling. The lesson extends beyond electricity to any infrastructure or regulatory change announced in advance and affecting durable investment: event-study pre-trends that look flat in the outcome can coexist with large anticipatory changes in the capital stock.

This boxed comparison states which two objects must be compared to obtain the full policy effect, namely two long-run equilibria in each of which capacity is the free-entry response to the network in place:

(f1, k∗(f1))vs.(f0, k∗(f0)).\big(f^{1},\,k^*(f^{1})\big)\quad\text{vs.}\quad\big(f^{0},\,k^*(f^{0})\big).(f1,k∗(f1))vs.(f0,k∗(f0)).

In the note's terminology these are Scenario 1 and Scenario 3 (equations (38) and (40)), and their difference is the boxed quantity of equation (41).

The qualifier “with endogenous investment” applies to both sides, and it has bite on the second. The integrated side is observed, since actual capacity is the equilibrium under the actual network. The separated side is never observed, because the data before the opening contain a separated market with capacity built for integration, the hybrid state of Scenario 2. Reconstructing it is the reason for the structural model: dispatch (equations (22)-(27)) to map capacity into prices, free entry (equation (28)) to map prices into capacity, and the invariance of the investment cost recovered in equation (33).

In the stylized model the comparison is between the autarky equilibrium of equation (3) with no solar and the integrated equilibrium with price ccc and the solar quantity of equation (9), skipping the transition state of equations (12)-(15) altogether. The general principle is that a policy evaluation should compare equilibria that are each consistent with agents' optimal long-run responses, and not a post-policy equilibrium with a pre-policy disequilibrium.
